On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question either to the parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General or to the Acting Postmaster General. Has an order been passed having the effect of penalizing post office employees who are sometimes late for work by taking time off their annual holidays? If so, who thought up the order, and will it be cancelled?

speakeroldname: Mr. T. A. M. Kirk (Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the publicity that has been given to the recent order, I wonder if I might not give a brief but comprehensive reply to the hon. member.
A circular was issued. The purpose of the circular was to ensure that employees are treated uniformly in the various offices throughout the service. Where employees are late owing to unavoidable circumstances, such as breakdown in transportation, heavy snowstorms and items of that kind, every reasonable cognizance is taken of these features.
In the postal service punctuality is exceedingly important. If employees are not on duty on time, mails are delayed and deliveries are retarded. Punctuality becomes all the more important with the advent of the 40-hour week. In many industrial concerns if the employees are not on time, the gates are closed and they are not allowed to work for a certain period of the day.
We felt that the employees should know the penalties they are likely to suffer so that they can adjust their arrangements accordingly, rather than to have imposed a penalty without any previous notice. Only a very small minority of our people are affected, as the majority have an exceptionally good punctuality record.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

order, will those representations be considered by the government?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Postmaster General):

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister a question. Has he received any message or request from the province of Saskatchewan with regard to the disastrous flooding in that province? Are any arrangements being made to confer on the matter, to send assistance or anything of that sort?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps the best answer I can give to the hon. gentleman is to say that last night I received from the premier of Saskatchewan a telegram which reads as follows:
Flooding of communities and farm lands on province wide scale has created disaster of major proportions. Urge your government to declare national emergency and give assistance on same basis as made available to other parts of Canada where similar disasters have occurred. Prepared to send ministers of provincial government to

confer with you and your colleagues if you so desire. Situation urgent and immediate assistance would be appreciated.
I telegraphed the hon. gentleman this morning in the following terms:
Your telegram received late last night and I wish to assure you everyone sympathizes with all those affected by recent storms and flooding in your province. We have no information that would indicate shortages of immediately necessary relief supplies nor nature and extent of actual destruction.
In cases where federal aid has been extended the provincial authorities had taken the initiative in securing factual information. I suggest that much more such information is required before any discussion with your colleagues could be really helpful. Your government will no doubt be securing such information and may wish to supply it to us and we will give it the same consideration as was given to all previous cases.

Mr. Speaker, might I ask a supplementary question. Would the Prime Minister consider using the federal forces in Saskatchewan, officials in P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A., who know every part of Saskatchewan, also to look into this matter and give it immediate attention?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the factual information collected by the provincial authorities has been brought to our attention we will take the best possible measures of checking it in order to satisfy ourselves that it represents the facts with regard to what has occurred.

speechtext:

59. Departmental administration, $493,651.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a matter within his department which I feel is far from being conducive to the promotion of good citizenship and the spirit of Canadian-ism and which to a certain section of our Canadian population is even insulting, to say the least.
May I start off first by saying that the population of our country is made up of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people of different racial origins who either themselves came from different lands or whose parents or ancestors did so. They have different backgrounds, but these people have brought with them their skills and their cultures and each is making a contribution to the building of our nation and the development of our distinctive Canadian national culture. I say that the strength of Canada lies in the diversity of its population. Regardless of what may be our occupation, what church we attend or whence came our parents, one thing we have in common with our neighbours is Canadian citizenship. At the same time we are members of the British commonwealth of nations which is the greatest organization that the world has ever seen. Certainly it is the policy of the government, and I am sure it is the thinking of every hon. member and of the Canadian people generally, that Canadians regardless of their racial origin should be proud of their origin whether it be Scottish, Polish, Anglo-Saxon, Ukrainian, French, Irish, or any other, proud of the contribution that they are making to this country and proud of the fact that these things have brought us together to make us better citizens and Canada a better place in which to live.
Having said that, I should like to draw the minister's attention to applications for Canadian citizenship that have been made by prospective Canadian citizens of Ukrainian origin. In making such applications these people have stated that they were born in the Ukraine. I should like to read the part of the reply of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration which is pertinent to the point I wish to make. These people have been told:
I regret to inform you that Ukraine is not the name of a country. It refers only to a province or a territory. As the name Ukraine does not refer to the name of a country, it would not be correct to enter Ukraine on your application form as your country of birth.
It seems to me that this statement, contained in a document coming from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, is not only insulting to these applicants but also humiliating. It is not only insulting and humiliating to them as applicants, but I think that kind of statement is insulting to any person of that origin regardless of whether he lives in Canada or any other part of the world, and there are some 50 million of them throughout the world. When someone makes a statement to the effect that "Ukraine" is not the name of a country, such a statement is incompatible with history and certainly incompatible with present-day facts.
I am not going to go into the history of the Ukraine, but I should like to point out to the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration minister that in that country today there is a population of over 42 million people, that it comprises a territory larger than France, that it is a separate republic in the Soviet union and is a charter member of the United Nations. When I say it is a republic I should like to qualify that by saying that it is a so-called republic because we know that the people there are not free. But even the recognition that this country has received from the Russians has only been after many millions of people have died fighting for freedom. As recently as the 1930's millions of them were starved deliberately on directions from Moscow because they believed in freedom and wanted to separate themselves from the Russian empire. The Russians have not been able to suppress that spirit of freedom although they have tried to do so for many years.
To touch briefly on history, I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to what happened in the year 1863. The Russian government, by a special decree, ordered the printing of all books and newspapers in the Ukrainian language to stop. When the Ukrainians appealed this decision to the government the minister of the interior, at that time Count Valuev, replied:
The Ukrainian language never existed, does not exist and shall never exist.
That happened in the year 1863. Yet since that time, after millions of people have died for freedom in an effort to break away from the Russian tyranny, they have at least been given the recognition of being a separate republic and have been recognized as a charter member of the United Nations. May I also point out to the minister that as recently as the 20th of November, 1917, after the czarist empire crumbled, the Ukraine became independent. If the western world had realized at that time the significance of what was happening, and if these people who had been trying to obtain their freedom and did obtain it for a short period of time had only received support from the western world, the Ukraine today would not be a part of the Russian empire, and Russia probably would not be the menace she is to the western world and to Canada in particular.
These newcomers who came to this country especially after the last war probably feel more keenly about this matter than any other ethnic group in the country and one can appreciate their reasons. They are the ones who have actually witnessed the liquidation of masses of their fellow countrymen on directions from Moscow. In spite of pressure they refused to go back to the Ukraine from the displaced persons camps, and they consider themselves very fortunate indeed to


have been able to reach the shores of Canada and to be in a position to be able to make application for Canadian citizenship after spending some time here.
For such people in particular the kind of statement contained in the letter from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is indeed most humiliating. Knowing the minister as I do, I am sure if he had known what was taking place he would never have allowed such a letter to be written to these newcomers. I am sure of that. We all know that is not the minister's way of thinking.
How would he know?
All you have to do is talk to the minister on any occasion with regard to his attitude to Canadians generally.
Born in this country or otherwise?

So I draw this matter to the attention of the minister with the hope that this sort of thing will not be repeated and with the hope that the minister will see to it that these people will be given the privilege of naming their country of birth as the Ukraine when they are making application for citizenship, because it is in conformity with the actual facts as they exist today and in conformity with history. If the minister should agree to that, then I would also suggest that any certificates already issued be changed accordingly if the people concerned want to have them so changed. With this in mind, I hope the minister will be able to see fit to make the necessary changes.

I should like to deal with this point right away. First of all, I want to express my sincere regret. As the hon. member correctly stated, I was quite unaware that to this circular letter sent out as a receipt for applications for citizenship in cases where there have to be some corrections or additions made-and that very often happens-the sentence to which he referred was added. The sentence was substantially as he read it, and I do not think there is any special reason why I should read it. The words are slightly different but the sense is quite the same. I can imagine how the hon. member for Greenwood, who like me was born in this country, would feel if the Department of Citizenship and Immigration said to applicants who put Scotland as their birthplace, "In your application you say you were born in Scotland; as this name pertains to a territory, district or province rather than a country it is requested that you state the name of the country in which you were born".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about your own constituents?

My own constituents, as the hon. member knows quite well because he, like me, is a sea lawyer, except those people who immigrated into Newfoundland from some foreign country, were born in Canada.
I do not wish to be diverted from what I am saying about this matter now.
Do not divert him now.
You diverted yourself.

I said that if Scotland had been used instead of the Ukraine in this instance, there would have been indignation which would have reached the ears of the minister rather sooner than this did. I would say this practice is one for which I, as minister, am constitutionally responsible.
No such sentence ever appeared until a few months ago. It has been used only since I was minister. I say that because I do not want anyone to think I am blaming my predecessor or anyone else. I had not had this matter drawn to my attention before.
We knew it was you.

That is right; the responsibility was mine. I am not going to plead ignorance, though I was ignorant of it. I say, sir, it was an error that was honestly made by a very conscientious civil servant who would not knowingly hurt anybody anywhere. It was made, and it was made with the intention of helping the people who make these applications.
Now, it is within the knowledge of many hon. members that citizenship certificates are used very frequently for identification of one kind or another. It has been the experience of the department that sometimes questions are raised about where some places really are. As the hon. member for Vegreville correctly stated, for many years the Ukraine has been juridically part of other states bearing other names. It is my honest opinion it is an advantage to the holder of a certificate, in certain circumstances, to have the juridical name of the country in which he was born also on his certificate. I have consulted my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, about this matter and from now on any applicant who wishes to state that he was born in the Ukraine and nothing else, will not be requested to amplify that at all so far as the country is concerned.
I shall have a circular prepared as quickly as possible to indicate that it might be to the advantage of applicants to indicate that the part of the Ukraine in which they were born was, at the time of their birth, under the jurisdiction of, say, Poland, Czechoslovakia or
1955	3519
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration imperial Russia, or that it is now the Ukrainian S.S.R., or whatever the fact may be. However, no one will be required to say that; it will be entirely optional.
I do not want to mislead anyone. There is another question on the application form that has to be answered, and that is question No. 4. It says, "I am a subject or citizen of-", and there, of course, it is absolutely imperative that the applicant put what his juridical status is, however disagreeable it may be to him. If the nationality of which he is divesting himself is Polish or Czechoslovakian that would have to be put. In the case of many of these newcomers to whom the hon. gentleman has referred, they are stateless, and of course that is a proper answer if it is a truthful one. But so far as the place of birth is concerned, and that is all that is inserted on a citizenship certificate, it will be quite sufficient to give the name of the place and so on, and for the name of the country to say Ukraine, and nothing else.
Perhaps I should repeat that I think it might be of advantage, especially to those people who have cause to leave the country on visits, to amplify it a bit, but that will depend entirely on them and what they want to do. In the case of those who now possess a certificate, and who would like to have the certificate altered so as to indicate that their birth was in the Ukraine, the department will be happy to have that done just as quickly as it is possible after the receipt of the certificate. Now, that may not be by return mail because I would not want to hold up the current certificates while these corrections are being made. I am sure the hon. member for Vegreville would not want that either, but the corrections will be made just as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, there was a matter about which I wanted to ask the minister when last we discussed the question of immigration and dealt with the numbers who had come into Canada in recent years. I was coming to the point of dealing with the question as to the numbers of people who have left Canada in the last 10 years, since 1945. I realize that so far as the records of the department are concerned they might not reveal the entire picture. I have endeavoured to secure information on this subject as a result of investigations in the United States through departments of government.
If those records which I have are correct, they reveal a tremendous exodus taking place from Canada to the United States, which has even been accelerated to a degree in recent

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration years. According to the records of the minister some one million people have come into Canada since 1945, over a million.
It is about 1,200,000.

Yes. I should like the minister to let the house and the country know what records he has in this regard: first, the numbers of people who are Canadian by birth or naturalization who have left Canada year by year since 1945; secondly, what records has he as to the numbers of immigrants who have come to Canada since 1945, who have not stayed here long enough to secure nor have they secured naturalization but who have more or less used Canada as an intervening stopping-off place to enable them to be in a better position to establish themselves in the United States? So far as the latter figures are concerned, I know they are difficult to obtain.
I ask the minister whether or not the suggestion that has come to me, that the numbers of non-naturalized Canadians, in other words aliens who have stopped in Canada for a period of years and who have not taken out naturalization but have gone to the United States since 1945, would amount to about 240,000? I ask him what he has to say in that regard. If that be true, that number, together with the records which the minister has indicated concerning the numbers of Canadians who have gone to the United States, would appear to lead to the conclusion that for every million immigrants who come into Canada about 515,000 Canadians, or people who came in as immigrants, have in the same period emigrated to the United States. That is one of the serious problems that affect us in our country, and one that demands the serious consideration of those in authority.^ For, certainly, if Canada's population during the intervening years since confederation had not been depleted continuously by migration from this country, our population would be immeasurably greater than it is today.
By way of an aside, may I point out that only the other day I was reading the year book for 1868 in which the fathers of confederation estimated that by 1940, under normal circumstances, the population of Canada would be in excess of 41 million people- more than three times our population today.
I shall deal with several points at this time, because X do not wish to hold up the passage of the estimates, or to delay this general discussion. There is another matter in connection with immigration upon which I should like to secure information. I join with the hon. member for Vegreville, in the remarks he made a few moments ago.


I remember when the major portion of the first group of Ukrainian immigrants came to this country in the early years of this century. Today in the province of Saskatchewan the first immigrant of that race is still living. Through the intervening years I have watched the amazing record established by the people of Ukrainian origin, in their contribution to the building of a great Canadian citizenship. I know that people of that racial origin will be most happy with the announcement made by the minister concerning the rectification of applications, in accordance with the suggestion by the hon. member.
I should like now to ask a question connected with emigration. Has the minister any record to indicate that in the last year or year and a half large numbers of Canadian young men have appeared at immigration offices in this country and have been directed to the offices of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the purpose of having their fingerprints taken, so that they might go to the United States. This information has come to me from an official in the immigration branch-or, at least, who was in the immigration branch. I would ask the minister if, in fact, records are kept to indicate the numbers of young Canadians who have indicated their desire to go to the United States for the purpose of joining the United States army. I would ask the minister to deal with that question because, if my information is correct-and, having regard to its source, I have no doubt that it is-it represents a challenging problem and one that deserves attention.
The third phase in connection with immigration is this: Are we doing everything we can to secure desirable immigrants in parts of Europe and the Middle East? I have in mind particularly the state of Israel. While I was there last year one or two university graduates-one in particular, from Jordan- indicated their desire to come to Canada, and I took up the question with the department. Both these young men were of the Christian faith. When I asked what could be done to facilitate the sending of application forms to them, the reply I received from the deputy minister, Mr. Fortier, was to the effect that the department did not have complete facilities in Jerusalem for the necessary examination of prospective immigrants; and therefore it was regretted that the department was unable to consider the entry of anyone from there at this time.
The one referred to, in the reply received from the deputy minister, was a young man of high educational attainments and scientific skill. He was a graduate in science, and one who could have made a great contribution

to this country. I would ask the minister whether it is intended to expand the number of countries to which will be accredited immigration officers so as to enable entry of those who are considered desirable.
I shall now pass on to one other subject, and then I shall have concluded the questions I intend to ask 'the minister. I come now to the question of the Indian population.
Would the hon. member mind holding that question until we reach Indian affairs branch. It would make it much easier to reply if we were to proceed in that way.

I certainly shall. I shall not press the question now, because I do not want to do anything that would interfere in any way with facilitating the discussion of the estimates.
However, one other matter comes to my mind in connection with immigration. Are the applications for every applicant for naturalization checked by the mounted police before the grant of naturalization is made? I have in mind a certain person, whose name I shall give the minister, who made application for naturalization. When the police communicated with him to ascertain his record, about which there was some question, the answer he made was, "I have already got my naturalization certificate; there it is".
I suggest to the minister that if that course is being followed in other cases, then it constitutes a dangerous loophole, permitting the admission to the ranks of Canadian citizenship of those who, by reason of their communist background, should not be admitted to citizenship. I feel that every care should be taken to ensure that citizenship shall not be conferred upon those coming from lands where communist principles are followed. I refer to those who would come to Canada because of advantageous economic conditions but who, at the same time, would desire to retain their allegiance to a foreign philosophy. I believe strict and careful examination should be made in every case, and that no certificate of naturalization should be granted without full and complete examination of the antecedents of the applicant. There should be most careful scrutiny with a view to sifting out those who ought not to become citizens by reason of their communist activities. Careful scrutiny should be made of their past record, and we should have the assurance that when they come here they will not continue past activities.

Mr. Chairman, may I deal with these various points raised by the hon. gentleman before they are driven from my
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration mind by listening to another hon. member?
I should like to point out first that I think the hon. gentleman is allowing his Saskatchewan patriotism to carry him a little far. The first Ukrainian immigrant who came to Canada was Wasyl Eleniak who came to the constituency of Vegreville in Alberta, and is still living there at the age of 96. I had the great pleasure of sending him a message on his birthday anniversary the other day.

If the minister will allow me, he will remember it was mentioned in the classics that over the years several places have claimed to be the birthplace of Homer. I noticed that the Saskatchewan Star-Phoenix took that gentleman the other day and moved him, as I recall, into the province of Saskatchewan.

This emulation I think is worthy of both provinces, and I offer not the slightest objection to it.
To take the questions that I can answer most briefly first, to say that the immigration branch acts as an immigration department for the United States is not correct. If there is any paid servant of the taxpayers of Canada in the immigration branch who is conducting himself in that way I should like to have a report on him.
There is no suggestion of that.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to say that our branch was directing people to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
No.
If I misunderstood-

My hon. friend does not understand it at all. In the case of people applying to have fingerprints taken I said the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has suggested that they be taken by the mounted police, but there is no participation in any such thing, and it was never suggested in the remotest degree.

Well, all I can say is that if it had nothing to do with the immigration branch, the whole thing is a complete mystery to me. I never heard anything about it before, and if it has nothing to do with the immigration branch, I do not think I can reasonably be expected to give any answer about it.
To come to the question of immigration from Israel, I am very grateful to the hon. member for Prince Albert for raising the matter, because there does seem to be a good deal of misunderstanding about it, which I do not want to contribute to and
3522	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration which I sincerely hope I can remove, at least in part. Israel, like Canada, is a country seeking immigrants. Israel, like Canada, is trying to add to its population by immigration, and it has been our policy since the war-and I have no doubt it was before-not to go to countries of immigration to look for immigrants. In other words, we do not try to encourage immigration into Canada from Australia, from New Zealand or from South American countries that are seeking to get people, or from Israel. I thing I am betraying no confidences when I say that representations have been made to us more than once by the government of Israel to the effect that they would view with concern any attempt on our part to look to Israel for immigrants.
Now, that does not mean that anyone who lives in Israel is automatically excluded from Canada. There are many cases where families have been separated and where the husband may be in Israel and the wife here in Canada, or where the children or the parents may be there. We do try to provide through the legation which was recently established in Israel a very limited service to deal with humanitarian and compassionate cases of that kind; but we are not seeking immigrants from Israel. As a matter of fact I think I may say that our department, like all other Canadians, welcomes the peaceful development of Israel and we do not want in any way to compete with them for people, and I do not think it would be a friendly act to do so.
It may be that there are individuals in Israel who would very much like to come to Canada, but if we systematically encouraged that kind of movement I think it would be considered by the authorities there to be a regrettable interference with what they are attempting to accomplish.
Will the minister permit me to ask a question on that same subject? That of course is an understandable point of view, but there is a different consideration where families are concerned.
Oh, quite.

The grievances that have come to my notice with respect to emigration from Israel relate to relatives here who want to bring close relatives from Israel, and they are finding the greatest difficulty in doing so because apparently there is no machinery for dealing with that situation.

Of course, by close relatives I mean close relatives in the strictest sense.
I mean parents and children, not nephews, not cousins or collateral relations of any kind, because I suppose a great proportion of the


population of Israel have relatives somewhere in North America and if the net were widened at all it would not mean anything.
I am referring to close relatives.
In the same sense?

For example, the daughter is free to come but there is no way to see whether her medical or other qualifications, formal qualifications, can be met, and so it is impossible for families who have close relatives to be reunited.

I think that situation is improving a little and will improve quite a bit more when our mission there has really found its feet. Of course, it has just been established in the last few months, as hon. members know.
I now come to the question of migration to the United States. I suppose I can make an answer that strictly speaking, in the narrow sense of the term, it is not the business of the immigration branch at all, but I am not going to make any such answer. I was asked some questions about this upstairs and I gave a table which is to be found on page 61 of the evidence of the estimates committee dated Monday, February 28. It was derived from the United States statistics. The hon. gentleman suggested that this should be put on the record. I wonder whether I might have the consent of the committee to have the second paragraph on this page inserted in the record without reading it?
The table follows:

The figures for 1951 to 1954 were taken from a report prepared by the statistical branch of the United States immigration and naturalization service.
What is the total for 10 years?
The total for 10 years is 256,000.
And these are naturalized Canadians?

It represents Canadian citizens, whether native-born or naturalized. I am not really quite convinced that it is the net figure because, as everyone knows, particularly for Canadian citizens, and more particularly for Canadian-born citizens, there is the very greatest ease of movement back and forth across the border. I suspect that on many occasions someone is shown in these United States figures as having been a Canadian immigrant to the United States who goes there and perhaps spends a year, and then comes back, and is not registered as a returning Canadian resident in the United States but merely as a visitor over there, and therefore we do not get the net figure. The difference would not be very great.
Has the minister any figures to show the numbers who left Canada but were not naturalized?

I am coming to that. I do not think I have forgotten the hon. gentleman's question. I have no figures of any kind in which I would place the slightest reliance to show what number of immigrants or aliens, even though they were not recent immigrants but resident in Canada for some time, may have gone to the United States in the past 10 years. I would be incredulous of the figure the hon. gentleman gave. Two hundred and forty thousand strikes me as much too high in relation to what we do know about the increase of the population of Canada over this last decade.
However, I think we will be able, when the census is taken and we get the figures in 1956, by the process of taking the natural increase and the known figures for immigration to arrive at a pretty fair figure of the numbers who have been lost, not only to the United States, but to all countries, by every form of emigration. Of course, it will not be possible from the census to break them down, but we will get the global figure in that way. To be quite candid about it, this to my mind is one of the biggest advantages of having the census taken in 1956, but I do not think we will really have any firm idea of what the net effect on the Canadian population has been of the post-war immigration until we have the census figures. As a matter of fact, I would appreciate from any source any practical, workable suggestions for measuring the emigration from Canada. It would be of the greatest possible help to the planning of our department to have such figures. We try to get every bit
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of information we can, on which we can place any reliance. For a variety of reasons unless we establish inquisitorial methods, it is very difficult to get it, except in the way I have suggested when the census is taken.
To come to the other question asked by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), about the checking of the applications for citizenship: as I think all members of the committee know, an application for citizenship must be filed with the clerk of the court. That is prescribed in section 27 of the act. It must be posted by the clerk in a conspicuous place in his office, or as otherwise prescribed by regulation, continuously for a period of at least three months before the application is heard by the court. The purpose of that is not merely to check the possibilities of what, I hope, I will not be misinterpreted in describing in a general way as subversive tendencies, but also to check the ordinary police records of applicants for citizenship. As the committee knows, under the Immigration Act the minister has a certain responsibility if landed immigrants are convicted of crimes involving moral turpitude. It enables interested persons to make representations to the court. The onus is placed on the judge of deciding these questions of good character and potentialities for good citizenship of the kind mentioned by the hon. member.
It is no secret, I think-at any rate it will not be from now on-that the department does avail itself of the services of the R.C.M.P. for that purpose. It may be that once in a while, in an individual case, something may happen so that it is not done as it should be. I would be very much surprised if there were not a slip once in a while. I am sure the county judges who do this work all over this country-I can say this from my own recent personal knowledge because I recently wrote a circular letter to all of them and have had a series of most interesting replies from many of them-are taking a deep personal interest in this work. I am glad to say that I think most of them are more concerned about giving a little encouragement to these people to become good citizens than trying to find too many flaws in their records. But if there are serious flaws, we try to do our best to find them, and I think the judges do too.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to comment briefly on a question raised by the hon. member for Vegreville to which the minister has already made a reply. I do so because I think that the matter he raised is important beyond the technicalities involved. I am very glad that the minister has admitted that the department-I shall not use the words
3524	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration "was at fault"-certainly was not using good judgment in some of the letters that went out. The hon. member for Vegreville stated that it amounted to an insult to have the kind of letters that were written to applicants. The minister and others may have thought that a rather strong word, but in view of the circumstances I think that was well justified because there has been, I think, a tendency for a certain amount of double talk on this question of these nations that have lost their sovereignty. When one takes into consideration that only as recently as the 8th of July, 1953, which date has some significance in that it was fairly close to a national event which took place that summer, the Prime Minister himself, speaking to the all-Canada congress of the Ukrainian Canadian committee, used these words, I would like to place them on the record because I think they are rather important coming from the Prime Minister of Canada. In reference to the struggle for the independence of the Ukraine, he used these words:
There may be many setbacks and disappointments, but all who believe this world is presided over by a Divine Providence must believe that one day the Ukrainian people will find a solid basis for political and cultural self-expression under a government, which, because freely chosen, will freely represent them. Then the long night of oppression will be over.
I quote those words with approval. All through that speech made on that date the words "Ukraine" and "Ukrainian people" appear again and again. With that background and taking that into consideration, one can easily understand the disappointment and shock that a person would feel on receiving a letter from an official in the department of immigration informing him quite blandly and bluntly that there is no such place as the Ukraine.
No such country.

One can imagine the reaction of anyone who fell under similar circumstances. I believe that the minister has done himself a great deal of good today by having quite frankly and openly admitted that it was at least bad judgment and agreeing to have that change made. While on that subject, I think, because of the general interest in the question, it could be pointed out that when the minister referred to the political regions concerned, the impression should not be left that any large number-and certainly not the majority of the immigrants coming in recent years to Canada-of Ukrainian origin came from jurisdictions under the U.S.S.R., because that is not the case. As a matter of fact, at the end of the second world


war the Ukraine was partitioned, as hon. members know, into four separate regions. There was a part under the U.S.S.R., a part that came under Poland, another portion that came into Austria, and a part under Czechoslovakia.
Did the hon. gentleman say "the second world war"?

The first world war. That situation continued until the second world war. As a result of certain agreements into which we entered at Yalta and other places the situation came about whereby all the regions known as the Ukraine fell within the boundaries of the U.S.S.R.-not only the Ukraine, but at least a part of Poland and a good part of some other nations. When that came about, the great majority of those who left those regions, and for the time being were in a state of exile as displaced persons in Germany, France and other countries, were people who came from that area which had been under Austria and under Poland. There would be a minority, and probably a small minority, that would be from Russia proper, simply because of the fact that they could not get out. Under those circumstances I should not like the impression to be left that they came from the U.S.S.R. in the first place, because they did not. Therefore stating to a person that he must not use the word "Ukraine" as his country of birth is not asking that he state his correct nationality but, as a matter of fact, it is almost forcing him to state his wrong nationality by trying to force him into a region from which he did not come.
I am glad that matter is being cleared up. It has more effect in the long run, as I said, than has the technical matter involved. As the minister will realize, and as do all hon. members, the cold war has not ended and the forces of communism in the Ukraine and in Moscow are extremely anxious to obtain any material on which they can lay their hands, and on the basis of which they can make political hay or propaganda. It is matters like these which cause discontent and irritation-and quite justifiably so-which fall into their hands and which are built up and exaggerated to great proportions in order to discredit the democratic countries.
I believe it is a fortunate thing many of the countries of the free world, particularly Great Britain, have taken some steps in recent years which have brought to the side of the western nations and to the side of freedom the peoples of Asia. I think it should be stated at this time that the one great act of statesmanship performed by the government of Great Britain under the leadership

of Right Hon. Clement Attlee, when they granted independence to India, did more to tip the scales in favour of the free countries, so far as Asia is concerned, than did any other event since the second world war ended. One can imagine what kind of a field day the communists would have had at Bandung recently had it not been for the fact that Nehru and others were there to speak for the democratic world.
These things which may appear to be small on the surface and perhaps unimportant in the eyes of some people have projected themselves into the international sphere with an importance quite beyond that of their immediate effect in our own country. I think it is quite important that, from time to time when these matters arise, the minister be as cautious as possible and try to straighten the situation out before it creates resentment in the first place and before it becomes, in the second place, an excuse or a thin edge of the wedge for the communist forces, supplying them with something with which to make propaganda.
I think the minister is to be commended for the attitude he has taken today. I think the hon. member for Vegreville is to be commended for having brought this matter to the attention of the committee.
I think the minister is rather painfully aware-from the rather painful emphasis placed on a certain incident-of how easy it is to do something which causes resentment. In this case I think he has to a great extent retrieved himself by taking prompt and, in my judgment, reasonable action.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Dauphin. I agree completely with everything he has said. I must say that no one could regret more than I do that this action was taken. In fairness to the officials who took it, I feel I must say this. I do not object at all to the word "insult", but it was a most unintentional one. The moment the matter was drawn to my attention, the greatest regret was expressed by the officials concerned. These are devoted people who work extremely hard in this branch; and the last thing they want to do is to hurt the feelings of any Canadians, no matter from where they come.

In order that there may be no misunderstanding may I at this point say that, so far as I am concerned personally, I have found that we have received good co-operation from the officials of the department of immigration. I am certainly not trying to leave the impression that anyone intentionally tried to insult anyone. But that
6, 1955	3525
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is the reason I drew attention to the international phase of this situation. I think it is important that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration work rather closely together in order that the policy of the government on these matters may be clear.
May I be permitted just to continue for a moment or two and say that the same situation will arise in a short time with respect to other countries. There is that sector, as I have mentioned, of Poland which is now in the U.S.S.R. There are the Baltic countries which find themselves in the same situation. For the time being the department has ruled that any territorial changes made as a result of the second world war shall not be taken into consideration. That ruling is fine so far as it goes, but the dead hand of time has a tendency to condone the acquisition of territory by conquest. We have seen that thing happen. I hope the government of Canada will be alive to that situation and will not allow itself to fall into that trap in the future.

I am grateful, Mr. Chairman, to have at last been able to catch your kindly and benevolent eye. As a matter of fact, I have been waiting since last Friday to make a few remarks on this important subject of immigration. Usually under these circumstances there is a tendency for speeches to accumulate and to gather momentum; but I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I shall be brief in what I have to say here this afternoon.
I want to deal for a moment with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and its appearance before the committee on the estimates. I do so because I arrived on that committee late in the proceedings. My name was added to the membership when the departmental discussions were half concluded, with the result that I did not have an opportunity actually to take part in the important preliminary discussions which endeavoured to appraise the effectiveness of the committee method of handling the estimates of the various departments. I am also dealing with it briefly because I feel that this is an important innovation in our parliamentary procedure.
Unfortunately I came away from that committee feeling that we had not accomplished too much by way of settling fundamental difficulties and misunderstandings relating to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. From the extended discussion which has gone on with respect to this first item, I think it will be concluded that other members are of the same opinion.
In my opinion there are three reasons why the discussion in the committee on estimates
3526	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration was not as successful as it might have been. I am going to state those three reasons briefly and quite specifically. First of all-and there was some discussion on this point- I believe the committee felt somewhat inhibited because of the presence of the minister in a dominating role. I know the interpretation of the minister with regard to the work of the committee. He regards it as a miniature of the committee of the whole sitting on the estimates. Unfortunately, if that precedent becomes established where a department comes under censure by public opinion, there is a great possibility of the committee being substituted for a fullblown committee of inquiry, with the result that this estimates committee could become merely a whitewash procedure.

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate
very much to interrupt the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, for whom I have very great esteem, but he is a member of parliament senior to me and it does seem to me there is a rule of the house that a question which has been decided should not be further debated in the same session. The question of whether the minister should be a member of the committee was debated and decided by the house.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether you are going to restrict me in discussing this point in a general way. As I have already indicated, I think it is important that particularly the members of the house who took part in the proceedings of the committee should have an opportunity to give their viewpoints on the matter. I am not actually saying that the minister should not be permitted to be a member of the committee. I am merely indicating that, from my standpoint at least, one of the reasons why I feel the committee was not as effective as it might have been was that the minister was there in a dominating role. I have not sought to deny him the right to be a member of the committee. He, as a native of Manitoba, has all the geniality of most Manitobans, and from that standpoint he added much to the atmosphere of the committee. In fact on certain occasions during the discussions the minister, by flattery, cajolery and the general art of ingratiation, was able to create an atmosphere of considerable congeniality.
I think the effect was somewhat disarming because when a member of the committee like the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, a man of considerable discernment, indicates at the end of the discussions that he is completely satisfied with what has taken place, one becomes aware of the minister's skill so far as winning friends and influencing people is concerned. Unfortunately, however,


instead of the committee acting as a group conscientiously considering the many problems relating to immigration-they have been referred to here this afternoon and last Friday-the committee tended to become somewhat of a mutual admiration society.
That brings me to the second weakness that appeared in the committee. In my view it became a mutual admiration society because of the inability to call for persons and papers outside of the department.

I wonder whether the hon.
member would mind if I raised a point of order. This particular matter was debated and voted on, and therefore I think it is decidedly out of order to debate it at this time. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether you would see eye to eye with me on that point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I had intended to rise previously when the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration raised his point of order, but I thought the hon. member who had the floor was concluding his remarks. I must find that I agree with both points of order that have been raised, and I must ask the hon. member for Brandon-Souris to confine his remarks to a general discussion of the affairs of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, as we usually do on the first item of a department. I realize we are breaking new ground in that this is the first time a department's estimates have been considered in committee of supply after having been considered in an estimates committee.
At the same time, our rules have been well established over many years and they generally give us the opportunity of debating certain matters at the most opportune time. On the first item of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration we have one of the best opportunities to debate the policies and administration of the department. This is certainly not the best opportunity to debate the proceedings of the committee on estimates or the advisability or inadvisability of having a committee on estimates. Therefore I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to a discussion of the affairs of the department.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I shall abide by your ruling and will simply conclude this part of my remarks by saying that in dealing with the problems facing parliament in this day and age, when the business of the house is growing in complexity, unfortunately we tend to resolve the difficulty by shortening discussion instead of providing for new procedures and techniques that would bring about a broader, wider and deeper discussion of parliamentary matters. That is not in the best interests of the parliamentary processes, as many authorities

have said in recent days in writings on such themes as the passing of parliament and so on.
I turn now to a few general remarks on the department. Since the estimates committee met, I have had occasion to present two or three cases to the immigration department for its consideration. While there was an indication during the proceedings of the committee, if I may refer to that body, that the processes would be speeded up and matters expedited as the result of the representations made there, I have discovered that we still face the same difficulty of delayed decisions on certain immigration matters. There is the same confusion, the same pious platitudes referred to in the press, and the same tendency to talk around the point. With respect to one case dating back to 1953 I have received a reply from the minister reading in part as follows:
I am unable to state when these inquiries will be completed but you may be certain the officials concerned will do their utmost in the matter. I shall of course keep you informed of developments.
I have been receiving the same answer since March, 1953.
There is one specific point I should like to raise at this time relating to Chinese immigration. I am given to understand that the regulations relating to the migration of Chinese citizens into Canada apply to Chinese-American citizens in the same way as they do to any other prospective oriental immigrants.
It is persons of Chinese race.

Persons of Chinese race.
Well now, that leads me to make another brief comment on the lack of lucidity in departmental policy. According to the general statement of 1947 one of the major categories in determining who were eligible to migrate to Canada was this factor of not altering the fundamental character of the people. It is difficult to know what is meant by "fundamental character". It is difficult to know whether it means race, culture or the other characteristics that might be summed up in that phrase "fundamental character".
In the case of a Chinese American citizen, of course, there is no difficulty of assimilation because his background is largely American. He has been educated in American schools; he thinks as an American, and there is no difficulty whatever from the standpoint of assimilation or from the standpoint of cultural conflict. It would appear, therefore, that one interpretation of this very vague definition of policy is definitely discriminatory on the basis of race. I should like to submit that that is not a very enlightened policy in the year
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration 1955 when the world has become a veritable whispering gallery, and when we are faced with all these sociological threats of the atomic era.
I shall bring my remarks to a conclusion, Mr. Chairman, by stating that last evening we listened to a very comprehensive discussion of the immigration problem by the hon. member for Cartier. There is no need for me to repeat the many excellent points he raised in that discussion, but I think it is a speech that deserves the consideration of the department. Certainly he set forth a much more vigorous, much more visionary policy for 1955 than the studied vagueness of the 1947 policy which it would seem the department is still following.

I have no desire at all at this time to hold up the estimates of this department. I must say that, by and large, I have had very good co-operation from the immigration officials. I have found them most co-operative when cases had merit and when there was some justification for bringing people into Canada.
But there is one particular case that has caused me a great deal of concern. I have written a great many letters and done a lot of telephoning in connection with it. I am not sure it has been brought to the minister's attention. The case concerns a family that I knew very well in Shanghai, China. In my opinion, they were good citizens. I believe their origin was central European, and they had a very good business in Shanghai. The family consisted of the parents, who were middle aged, a daughter who was married and the son in law. The daughter and her husband came to Canada a few years ago and settled in Vancouver. They would have brought the parents at that time but they were not in a financial position to pay the passage and, in any event, they had no place in which to settle.
These people have now become well established in Vancouver, and are endeavouring to bring the parents to Canada. Since Canada has no representative in China, I believe communication is had through the British consul situated in Shanghai. Application has been made to the British consul and a Canadian visa has been obtained. The parents have had their medical and have all assurances that they can come to Canada, but they are unable to get an exit permit from the Chinese government. My opinion is that they have never been able to get their case understood by the right authorities in China, because there would be no logical reason for the Chinese government keeping them there. They will never contribute anything to the national life, and they are only consumers.
3528	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I would suggest that the minister might use a little influence with the British consul in an attempt to show the Chinese government that these people should be permitted to come to Canada. I do not know whether or not that is regular, but I feel sure that these people are not able to get their request understood by the proper Chinese authorities. As a matter of fact, I would not mind writing to Chou En-lai myself if I thought he would ever get the letter or that it would do any good. I suggest that something along that line could be done, because these people are very anxious to have their parents come to Vancouver. They are well established and able to provide for them, and the family should be united if at all possible.

I am in somewhat the same position as the previous speaker, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to hold up these estimates, but this committee is the only place that I can get an answer to a certain question. I should like to ask the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, how one proves he is a Canadian citizen. I ask that question because about two months ago the department under the control of the minister sent to all members I presume-I received one anyway-a certain communication.
I want to refer to the introduction. I do not know what to call it, Mr. Chairman, because there is no heading on it. The communication has these words at the bottom of it, "Department of Citizenship and Immigration; Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, minister; Laval Fortier, deputy minister". I am not going to quote all of it, but it says this:
As a convenience to Canadian citizens, who wish to have a certificate of citizenship which can be carried easily with them, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration now has available a miniature certificate which fits into wallet or purse.
Hear, hear; that is right.

Yes. Farther down, the communication reads:
The application form, (C.R.l), which may be obtained from any clerk of court or from the registrar of Canadian citizenship, Ottawa, must be fully completed by the applicant, sworn to before a notary public, commissioner for oaths or justice of the peace, and sent together with the statutory fee of $2 to-
And so on. I have not replied to this as yet because the communication says this form C.R.l must be fully completed. At the same time as I received the communication I got a copy of form C.R.l. Here is form C.R.l. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think I am a Canadian citizen. At least, I was a member of the British Columbia legislature for 20 years, I have been here for two sessions, and no one has yet challenged that fact. If it is correct
[Mr. MacKenzie.l

that form C.R.l must be fully completed, then I say the reason I have not done so is that it is impossible for me to do it. It is absolutely impossible. So I am asking this question. Here is form C.R.l, and we will start on the first page. "My place of birth is"-O.K., I can prove that; I have my certificate. Then, "My date of birth is"-yes, I can prove that, because I have my birth certificate. Then, "My occupation is"-you know, that has me a bit stumped.
It never bothered me.

It won't after the next election, either. I am an electrician by trade, and I sign that way. But for 22 years I have been an elected member.
Then, "Years of experience"-
May I ask a question?
Sure.
What occupation did he put on the ballot paper?
"Electrician".
Well, that would be satisfactory.

Fine. It says, "State any other occupational skills". Do I say "M.P."? However, that is only by the way. But these questions can bother an awful lot of people.
And now I am coming to the important part -because I was not born in Canada, I was born in England. The minister is shaking his head, because he does not know what I am coming to. But you will shake your head the other way when you do.
Now, look, almost underneath this, on the front page, it says, "I am a Canadian citizen by"-well, I can come only under two of these classifications, namely (B) (C). We find that (B) says, "Birth outside of Canada. (See appendix A)". And then classification (C) says, "Being a British subject with Canadian domicile, or by maintaining a place of domicile in Canada for 20 years immediately before January 1, 1947. (See appendix B)".
I could come under only those two classifications. All right; now let us turn to the back page, to appendix A and appendix B- and I am not being facetious about this, at all. I am only referring to it because of this document-which I cannot properly name- which says that form C.R.l must be fully completed if I want to have proof that I am a Canadian citizen.
O.K.; let us now look at appendix A and appendix B-because I must come under

either one or the other. Let us look at appendix A. Well, sir, I can answer only one question in appendix A-and I have no proof of even that one. I can answer it only because I honour my father.
What is the first question? It is this: "My responsible parent"-yes, "my responsible parent"-I honour my father. I will answer it that way. But I always thought it took two to have me born.
It only takes one to make you a Canadian citizen.
Maybe so, but it takes two to have me born. So, who is "my responsible parent". Is it my mother or is it my father?
I think I had better answer the hon. gentleman now.
Oh no, let me go ahead.
I do not know whether the hon. member wants an answer.
Let me go ahead; answer later.
He is only wasting time.
I beg your pardon?
I said you are only wasting time.
Well, I don't think I am wasting time for the mothers and fathers of this country when I question having to answer who "responsible parents" are.
Maybe we will find out what babies the minister was talking about in Victoria.

I don't think I am wasting time. Now, this is something!-"My responsible parent". You know, it hit me as being wrong, as soon as I saw it. You ask me who my responsible parent is. That was an absolute insult, as soon as I saw it.
Well, would the hon. gentleman let me answer.
You can answer after I am through.
Certainly, and I shall be glad to.

"My responsible parent"-O.K.; let us go on after that. I come now to this: "Who was admitted to Canada on"-well, I know I came here in 1910. But, according to this, I cannot tell you the date, nor can I tell you the port of entry or the ship. In fact, I cannot tell you anything that would have to be answered in appendix A-except that my dad is Ernest Winch. That is all I can tell you. So, in this document you sent
6, 1955	3529
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration around to us a few months ago, which says that appendix A must be fully completed, I cannot answer the questions.
Then, suppose we go on to appendix B which, first of all, asks me to "Give full particulars of your entries and departures". Then it states "First arrival at"-and then there is a space for the "port", the "date" and the "ship".
Sir, in appendix B I cannot answer one single question.
You could find out if you wanted to.

Time after time, in old age pension applications, we hit this question: When did you arrive at the port of entry, on what ship and on what date? And it cannot be answered. I cannot answer it, to get my own little card that I would like to have; because it says here that I must fully complete this document. I would say that to complete it would be almost an impossibility for the great majority of people born outside of Canada.
So I would ask the minister now-and he has been jumping up several times-to explain how you prove you are a citizen, under your orders, when it is impossible to complete the document that you say has got to be filled out in full.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman shares with me and with a few other new members the distinction of having had no part in defining the phrase "responsible parent", because neither he nor I was here when the act was passed. However, most members in the house helped to pass the Canadian Citizenship Act; and if before making his speech this afternoon, the hon. gentleman had looked, as I should have thought, as an experienced legislator, he would have done, at the legislation upon which this document is based, he would have found that the expression "responsible parent" is defined in the interpretation section.
I do not think there is need for me to waste the time of the committee in reading the section, because most hon. members helped to put it through parliament.
But, of course, that is not the point at issue. If the hon. member had read the document at all carefully he would have seen that all he needed to do to establish the fact that he is a Canadian citizen was to indicate, as he has indicated today, that he was a British subject and had resided in Canada for 20 years before January 1, 1947. And, having done that, no other proof of any kind would have been necessary.

"And", "and", "and"-sign appendix B. Come on, now-sign appendix B; that must be done. And I cannot answer appendix B-I cannot answer one question in it.
Well, if the hon. gentleman would send me his birth certificate I would have the form filled out for him, and save him the trouble.

O.K. But it is not going to stop there, because I am not interested myself. I know that, without doubt, I could have gone to my friend and got my certificate. I am talking on behalf of the thousands of people in Canada who get this form and do not know what to do with it; I am not worrying about myself.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, on that point, the hon. gentleman read in the circular that the thing to do was to go to the clerk of the court. I think he would find that any clerk of the court would be willing to help him. I admit that some of the language sounds a little silly. I shall have a look at it to see whether we can improve it.
And the questions are stupid.

Perhaps there is something more than merely faulty language to it. I had the same reaction as the hon. member for Vancouver East and I was in the same position myself. I could not tell you what port I landed at or the date on which I landed. I was a child at the time. It is getting close to 50 years ago. But there are quite a lot of people in Canada who might have very serious difficulty in proving to you that they were qualified under that section. They were born in Britain; perhaps they had a British birth certificate. They might not even have that, and they might have great difficulty in proving that they had lived in Canada for the sufficient length of time. 1

That of course was one of the reasons why the 20-year rule was put in. It was to obviate that kind of difficulty. If there are any serious difficulties of this sort I shall be very glad indeed to give consideration to them. I recognize that the hon. member for Vancouver East is having a little fun at my expense.
No, sir.

But I think that most of us, myself included, have difficulties, even though I have not the difficulties of either of the hon. gentlemen who have just spoken, but I have some others. I am allergic to forms. I hate filling them out. I get my secretary to do it, and she seems to know how. I do think there is a great deal to be said for simplifying those


forms in any way that that can be done; but there is an inherent difficulty. When you live in a country as we do, a country with immigrants from all quarters of the earth, the number of variations of experiences is so great that it is very hard to get a simplified form that will elicit the first time all the information that is necessary, and you have to balance, on the one hand, asking too many questions, and sometimes too complicated questions, against on the other hand having to write a second letter, which is also very annoying to applicants.
I understand that and, Mr. Chairman, please, I am not trying to embarrass the minister.
I do not suggest that; I know you are just having fun.

No; it costs almost $6,000 an hour to keep the House of Commons in session, and I am not having fun and will never have fun at that expense. Did the minister know-and this applies to members of the House of Commons-that under his name the form says that C.R. 1 has to be fully completed in order to get your registration and your certificate as a Canadian citizen, and did he know what it entailed because, sir, I cannot answer completely any of these questions?

I do think that we who were, shall I say, unfortunate enough not to have been born in Canada and at the same time to have been born in the British Isles are in a rather anomalous position in Canada. We are, you know, Mr. Chairman, rather in the position of the man who said he was the only person in the gallery who had a certificate to prove that he was sane.
That was in the house.

Well, sometimes I have felt that we are almost in a worse position than the other people who were born in Germany, in Italy, or anywhere else. They have a certificate to show that they are Canadians, but we who were born in the British Isles are sort of left floating in the air. It is rather difficult for us to prove our status. The minister should examine the wording of the act. Perhaps it may have to be amended to clear up the position of people like ourselves. It is simple enough for individuals like the hon. member for Vancouver East and me; we can prove it, but there are a lot of people who cannot.

May I bring to the attention of the minister the problem of young people born to naturalized Canadians but of foreign birth? These young people grow up and attend our Canadian schools and universities. The

young graduate from time to time finds lucrative employment in the United States or in some other country. Many employing companies feel that these young people will remain employed much longer if they become citizens of the country in which they are working, and often pressure is exerted on them to this end; consequently, they give up their citizenship. At this time I know that a number of these young people would like to return to Canada, but they hesitate to do so because they are required to wait five years before attaining Canadian citizenship again. May I recommend to the minister that this class of people be regarded as those coming within the one-year residence requirement for citizenship. I believe that these former Canadians will prove to be a great asset from the experience they have gained outside of Canada. This matter comes to my attention rather forcibly because only this week I had a senior class of boys from a Chatham school. This school was represented by seven different language groups. I believe the situation also comes about because of our close proximity to the United States border.
That is a provision of the law now. If they are natural-born Canadians it does not matter who their parents are.
These young people came to this country with their parents, who were of foreign extraction.
They were not bom in Canada.
That is correct.
The provision is only for natural-born Canadians.

A great deal of emphasis has been placed on some statistics in this debate in regard to questions relating to date and port of entry, and so on. I have had occasion to handle dozens of applications for citizenship for various people from various parts of the world in my constituency. In the majority of cases they do not know their port of entry or the exact date of entry and other related details; but I have always found that as long as the basic qualifications for citizenship are established the department has never refused an application on the ground that this information is not available.

I will be brief, Mr. Chairman. The minister and the officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration have a great job to do in settling all the differences that come to them from every country in the world. Like the hon. member for Kent, Ontario, I have had something to do with the officials of the department and 50433-223J

I know I wanted two Chinese boys out in Fort William whose fathers were citizens of Canada, and I have not been successful in getting them in yet, but the fight is still on.
The reason I rose was to say that I tried for two years to get a family out from Poland. They were Hebrews or Jews. We got them out, and that family has been a credit to the country they came from and an asset to Canada. The boy and girl have now graduated from the university and they paid me the great honour at Christmastime of addressing me as Rabbi Dan Mclvor. I have a case now that bothers me, and I tell the minister that I am not going to let go. The young man in question has a father and mother, uncles and aunts and brothers and sisters in Fort William. He did a bad deed, but of course the temptation was not considered. He is now to be deported. His case should be reconsidered. I am sure that the parish priest and I will go good for the conduct of that boy in the future. It is not fair to punish his family by sending him out of Canada. He is now in Guelph. I can give the full particulars to the minister, and I shall keep on trying for his answer. I ask that this case be reconsidered, and not ended, as the letter which I received today indicated.

There is one statement I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. I always like to be absolutely honest. I do want it known that since I first came here as a result of the election on August 10, 1953, I have had a number of immigration cases. I ran into trouble on most of them. I want to say, because I think it is only fair to say it, that since the present minister has been in his post he has reviewed all the cases I have drawn to the attention of his department since I first came here. All have been adjusted by him, with the exception of one, and it is not his fault that this last one has not been adjusted. I want to say that I have had the finest co-operation from the minister and all cases have been satisfactorily adjusted.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make it plain at the outset that anything I might say is not with the idea that I am opposed to immigration. I am not opposed to immigration. I realize that all our forefathers were immigrants at some time, and some of them were even more than immigrants; they took over this country by brute force. The only genuine Canadian babies are the Indians and Eskimos in our country.
I should like to add one little matter to a point that was raised by the hon. member

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration for Vegreville and the hon. member for
Dauphin. When Canadians, even though they have been in Canada for a good number of years and are naturalized, happen to go to the United States just for a day or so, one of the first things they are asked is "Where were you born?" If the answer is, "Well, where I was born is now under the jurisdiction of the Soviet union", we find that Canadian citizens are at times unduly subjected to unnecessary interrogation. I believe that if adequate representations were made by the minister in co-operation with the Secretary of State, that difficulty might be eased somewhat.
Many of those people came to Canada many years before what is now the soviet regime had control over their territory. A matter I wish to speak on is this problem of whether immigrants cause unemployment.
I think most Canadians might say it has not been proven that immigration causes unemployment. However, I think that depends on what type of immigration we have into Canada. In looking at our Canadian population we see that out of some 15 J million people, some five million are in the Canadian labour force. In other words some two-thirds of our population-67 per cent of Canadians-who are not in employment could be classed as dependents. If we want to show that immigration does not cause unemployment, then I believe the same ratio would also have to apply to our immigrants. However, if we take a look at our statistics we find, for example, that in the year ending March 31, 1953, less than 46 per cent of the immigrants were classed as dependent wives or dependent children. I think the figure for last year is about the same.
I believe that is a clear indication that we are not receiving the average family such as we have in Canada. I think the percentage of single people entering Canada looking for immediate employment is far out of line. I often wonder whether these immigrants have no wives and children, and how it is that often much more than half our immigrant population seeks and obtains direct
