employment. I think the possible origin of this wrong percentage stems from the fact that it seems to be the policy of the government to lay down rules and regulations under which immigrants may come to Canada if they wish.
I feel that is a wrong attitude to take.
I think our Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, with his cabinet colleagues, should decide on what immigrants the Canadian economy needs and then should actively pursue a course to see to it that we obtain these immigrants. They should not merely lay down rules and regulations and have a staff of civil servants administer them and leave it to the employers in Canada. Often employers look for immigrant labour because they can for a limited time obtain that labour at lower wage rates. I agree that we need a greater population in Canada, but I am also convinced that it is up to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to make sure we do obtain the immigrants we wish.
The hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned possible immigration into Canada from Israel. I understand that there are almost three-quarters of a million displaced persons immediately outside Israel. If we need more people in Canada, and I agree that we do,
I sometimes wonder whether such a wealthy nation as Canada could not undertake such measures to relieve some of the serious tension that exists there. We all know that when the state of Israel was formed, roughly three-quarters of a million people of Hebrew origin flooded into that state. At the same time almost the same number of natives of Israel left the land and are today, and have been for years, looked after by the United Nations. The Arabic nations around the borders of Israel do not want these people to become permanent residents, and the state of Israel, naturally enough, does not want the people of Arabic origin to re-enter Israel and become settled there.
When I look at the table for the year I previously mentioned I notice that in that year we admitted 4,539 immigrants of Hebrew origin. People of Syrian origin are listed as 184. People of Arabic origin are listed as 70. When there is a camp-a future trouble spot-with three-quarters of a million displaced persons, and from those displaced persons as well as the four or five nations around Israel we admitted only 254, I hardly think we are doing everything we might do.
My main reason for rising in this discussion of the first immigration item in the estimates was to protest immigration policy in regard to citizens of India. I believe the same would apply to citizens of one or two other nations

near India. I believe we have an agreement with the government of India and one with the government of Ceylon-and, I think, with one or two other similar nations-whereby we set a limit on the number of immigrants Canada will take. We do not set such a limit on other regions of the world, even on some of the other coloured regions of the world.
I feel that the continuance of this quota arrangement is not in the best interests of our nation. I agree that no matter how wide we opened the door to orientals or to immigration from India we would not ease the severe overpopulation and economic hardships over there. However, by the very fact that we have a quota we are showing racial discrimination. Whether we are prepared to admit it or not, it is nothing short of racial discrimination, and it is keenly resented by these people. I realize that the quotas may have been agreed to by the governments of those countries, but we have quite a few of those people living within our nation. They are showing themselves to be good citizens, and they deeply resent this racial discrimination.
Then, I do not like the harsh interpretation of the immigration laws and the way they are being applied to relatives of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin. I think we are being unduly afraid lest there enter Canada in any one year 100 or 200 Chinese more than we are obliged to admit. I think we are being overly cautious. I would not think that a great catastrophe would happen to Canada if one citizen of China was able to enter the country and settle in each of our ridings, or a total of 265 who, under our present system of law enforcement with regard to the Immigration Act, would not be allowed in. Catching the chairman's eye has involved much greater physical activity this afternoon than I had counted on, and I am happy to have achieved my object. My remarks are going to be along a somewhat different line. I have a question or two to ask on policy in connection with immigration, but I think I shall save them until we come to the immigration branch, to which I think the minister quite wisely has been wanting to get.
What I have to say now concerns in a general way the value the House of Commons is receiving from the work of the estimates committee. I am not going over the debate we had in the house on that matter. I am just offering some suggestions. For example, at page 426 of the report of the estimates committee, considering the estimates of the department of immigration- and this is to be found in proceedings No. 14-the minister used these words:
I imagine that it would not be reasonable to ask the committee of supply to consider this department until the proceedings of this committee are all printed, because it would not be fair to the members who are not here, and it would not save the time that we wished to save by this procedure.
Quite right. This department did not come before the committee of supply until the proceedings were printed. But here is my objection, Mr. Chairman. If the committee on estimates is going to be continued another session I think those who take cognizance of these matters should consider very carefully some method of making it possible for interested members to find in the reports of the proceedings what items have been discussed. I spent a considerable length of time in endeavouring to locate in these various volumes the answers with respect to


a problem in which I am particularly interested, and it was like searching for a needle in a haystack. I knew the number of the item I wanted to find, but how do you find it in 14 volumes of proceedings?
It surely will be necessary for some index to be put at the front of these volumes. Surely it will be necessary to print in a heading the number of the vote being considered and the title of the vote, just as is done in Hansard. For example, when we started the consideration of this department the following information was set out at page 3290 of Hansard of April 29:
Department of Citizenship and Immigration
59. Departmental administration, $493,651.
You cannot find anything like that in the reports of the proceedings of the estimates committee. I shall give three examples. At the second line on page 293 of the reports of the committee the chairman said:
We are on items 66 and 68 of the estimates.
A member of the house who was not a member of the committee has to look at the estimates book to see what is dealt with by these items. If you look at page 385 you find in the second line that the chairman said:
We are on the items numbered 70 to 80 inclusive in the estimates of the Indian affairs branch.
Suppose a member was interested in item No. 74 under "welfare of Indians, operation and maintenance"; how would he locate it? Well, you find it at page 409 of the proceedings of the committee, about 20 lines down from the top of the page where the chairman says:

If we are to gain anything by the work of the estimates committee when that committee reports back to the house, the reports of the proceedings of the committee should in some way make it possible for members to find quickly where items were discussed in that committee and the topics that were considered. If the items were set out in that way and could be referred to rather easily I would think a minister might be saved some effort in making his replies here. It might even be a minister who is more reticent and somewhat less loquacious than the hon. gentleman who is responsible for this department, but I make this suggestion as an aid to the minister concerned who might say that the question the hon. member was raising could be found answered completely at such and such a page in the proceedings of the estimates committee, and that he had nothing further to add. The converse is also true. Later I intend to suggest that at such and such a page of the proceedings of the committee the minister's answer to a certain

question raised there was not complete and needs to be elaborated on this occasion.
I quite freely offer these suggestions to those in charge of preparing documents for the use of members of the House of Commons. I hope they will endeavour to prepare something for the future that will make it much easier for members of the house and others interested in these topics to find the information they would like to have.

AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 304, to amend the Small Loans Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to provide for a reduction in the maximum interest rate that may be charged by small loans companies in Canada from 2 per cent per month to 1 per cent per month. It is now 16 years since parliament dealt with the interest rates that may be charged by small loans companies. In 1939 parliament placed the present ceiling of 2 per cent per month for the first 15-month period of the loan on interest rates that may be charged by small loans companies, and reduced the rate to 1 per cent per month after the initial 15-month period has elapsed.
The purpose of the bill is to reduce the 2 per cent maximum to 1 per cent and make the maximum ceiling 1 per cent per month for the whole period over which the loan may be repaid.
The interest today, as I said, is 2 per cent per month or 24 per cent per year. I believe that just stating that maximum should itself be almost sufficient to convince members of this house that this rate is too high. I suggest that 24 per cent per year is a fantastically high rate of interest, and it is certainly monstrous that Canadians who have to obtain small loans should be forced to pay such a very high and exorbitant interest rate.
From time to time one reads of the high interest rates that prevail in many countries in Asia and Africa. We read of interest rates prevailing there of 24 or 25 per cent per year and up to 50 per cent per year. Our reaction to reading that such a thing does occur is, is it not wonderful to live in Canada where we do not have to pay such high interest rates? The fact is, however, that hundreds of thousands of Canadians are continuously paying interest rates of 24 per cent per year, and in many instances interest rates very much higher than 24 per cent.
I intend to have something to say about those much higher rates when on a later occasion I move a bill standing in my name which deals with interest rates. I will, however, say to the house at this time that there are prominent business firms in Canada today, some of our biggest, that are charging interest rates on instalment buying up to as high as 54 per cent per year. When we speak, therefore, of the exorbitant rates prevailing in certain countries of Asia and Africa we should not be horrified, because such rates are currently being charged in Canada.

Small Loans Act
Over the years I believe the trend has been to reduce interest rates. It has been the more or less consistent policy of the government in power to endeavour to get the rate of interest down, and make credit and money more easily available. We now have a prevailing rate of interest on government bonds in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent, and in all instances I believe less than 4 per cent. The large sums of money that are now lent under the National Housing Act are being lent at a total interest rate of 5-25 per cent per year. The interest rate charged under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, about which I shall have something to say later, is 5 per cent per year. The regular rate of interest charged to people who borrow various sums of money from the banks is generally in the neighbourhood of 5 or 6 per cent.
Surely it is the job of members of parliament to study the Small Loans Act and the legislation pertaining to small loans companies and their practices, to see if we cannot do something to reduce the maximum of 24 per cent per year, which is four times as high as the interest rate charged on most loans obtained from our banking institutions. Members of this house should bear in mind that the people of Canada who accept loans from these small loans companies are, by and large, the people least able to afford such a high rate of interest. The job of government should be to make the rates that apply on loans to low income people as nearly as possible comparable to the rates that may be charged to people who are considered better risks. No matter what argument may be advanced as to the difference that must prevail in the rates, I suggest that the wide difference between the 6 per cent on ordinary bank loans and the 24 per cent on small loans is a drastic difference about which parliament should do something.
This is not the first time the C.C.F. party has advocated such a reduction in interest rates. As a matter of fact, when the legislation now on the statute books was introduced and passed by parliament in 1939 an amendment was moved and seconded by the present hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Their amendment asked that the maximum rate be reduced from 2 per cent per month to 1 per cent per month, as is provided in this bill. It went even farther and asked that the 1 per cent rate which prevails after the loan exceeds a period of 15 months be reduced to one-half of 1 per cent per month.
In the hope that this legislation might be more acceptable to all members of the house I decided that it might not be wise at this

time to advocate that the 1 per cent be reduced to one-half of 1 per cent after 15 months, even though such a move might be desirable. I felt rather that the bill should be confined to something so reasonable that all members in all parts of the house could give it their full support. I want to point out that the credit unions in Canada are lending very large sums of money to their membership at a rate of 1 per cent per month. They are doing that successfully. They are covering all their expenses, and are able to declare a saving from time to time.
I should like to quote a short paragraph from an article written in the Canadian Unionist entitled "Desjardins States his Philosophy", by Ralph S. Staples, president of the Co-operative Union of Canada. This article, as is suggested by the title, deals in the main with the Desjardins philosophy and the great contribution he made to public life in Canada by promoting and fostering the original credit unions of this nation. The paragraph reads as follows:
Already there are nearly 4,000 credit unions in Canada, with about 1-5 million members holding assets of about half a billion dollars and loaning well over $200 million to their members each year. The number of credit unions and the scope of their operations is growing rapidly. Only five years before, in 1948, credit unions numbered 2,600 and the membership was 850,600.
As I say, the credit unions have operated successfully on an interest rate of 1 per cent per month, and I suggest to members of the house that such a ceiling is indeed reasonable. I believe that the provision of credit is very important to any progressive nation, and that much of our prosperity at any given time depends upon Canadians being able to meet their credit needs readily and at reasonable interest rates.
Most of the loans that are obtained from the small loans companies, I suggest, are obtained for good purposes. They are obtained by the mother or father of a family, usually for the purchase of needed clothing, furniture for the home or in other instances to meet bills of an emergency nature.
Someone may say, "Well, these people should not be obtaining credit". But I suggest that in practice the average Canadian uses credit as a means of making a saving. That is, he obtains at one time a reasonable sum of money for the purchase of a given article, and arranges to repay the loan in instalments. At the end of the period of the loan he has made a saving, as represented by the article purchased when the loan was obtained. I suggest that the refrigerators, pianos, electric stoves, chesterfield suites and main items of household furniture in the majority of the homes in Canada have been obtained on some basis of credit-perhaps

through a loan from a small loans company or, in other instances, by being purchased on a credit or instalment basis. And I believe that kind of practice should not be frowned upon. It is going to go on in any case, because people on low incomes are going to have to go without many of these items unless they can obtain reasonable credit.
That being the situation, I should like to see this legislation enacted, whereby such loans could be obtained at reasonable rates. As a matter of fact the kind of interest legislation we have in our nation today is class legislation. There are high interest rates for the low income groups and low interest rates for the high income groups. I am not suggesting that those rates can be equalized, but I do say that the difference in those rates at the present time is far too great. We should attempt to bring them closer together by reducing the maximum rates that may be charged by small loans companies.
Present legislation makes provision for a maximum loan of $500. I might have placed another section in the bill which would have increased the ceiling on what might be termed a small loan. I think if such provision were in the bill it would be a good one, because I would like to see the $500 ceiling greatly increased. It should be increased from $500 to shall we say $1,200, if it is to be kept in the same general terms as the 1939 act from the standpoint of purchasing power. Perhaps it should be $1,500, because even $1,500 in 1955 in many instances will buy very little more than could be bought for $500 when the legislation was enacted in 1939.
But even this, I suggest, is not going far enough. Perhaps the ceiling should be placed as high as $3,500, and I do not pick this amount at random. Rather I take it from section 75 of the Bank Act, which now provides that a bank may lend up to $3,500 and take security by way of a chattel mortgage. I suggest if it is found, for the purposes of the small loans departments of chartered banks, that a figure of $3,500 is reasonable, then in legislation of this kind, designed to keep interest rates down to a reasonable level, we might consider increasing the ceiling on the so-called small loan to at least $1,500. I would go so far as to say that it might be preferable to bring the amount up to $3,500, as is provided in the Bank Act.
The small loans business in Canada has become more and more important over the years. I have some figures here that will demonstrate just what rapid growth there has been in the business of small loans. A table showing the interest earned on small loans by small loan companies shows that in 1941 the interest earned amounted to $1,642,000, that in 50433-224
Small Loans Act
1946 it had increased to $2,926,000, that in 1949, three years later, it had increased to $8,173,000 and that in 1953, the last year for which figures are available, the interest earned on loans by small loans companies in Canada amounted to $16,099,000, or an increase of 900 per cent within a period of 12 years.
These figures not only show the rapid growth of our Canadian economy, but show also that the growth of the small loans business has even exceeded the general expansion. The fact that the small loans business assumes such an important place in the economy of our nation offers a further reason why at this time we should give consideration to a reduction in the maximum interest rates.
To show what large sums are placed out on credit in Canada I have here the Bank of Canada statistical summary for March, 1955, which shows that outstanding in charge accounts at the end of 1954 was a total of $503 million, that instalment credit placed by retailers amounted at that time to $315 million, that instalment credit provided by finance companies amounted to $480 million, and that cash personal loans by chartered banks, small loans companies, licensed moneylenders and credit unions amounted to $665 million, making a total credit of $1,963 million. Without attempting to find out how many loans might be involved, assuming- and this might be far from the actual case- that loans amounted to an average of $1,000 each, we would find that two million persons had credit in one form or another at the end of 1954.
With general credit in such proportions and of such outstanding importance to the whole Canadian economy, I suggest it is wrong that the low income group should have to pay the exorbitant charges made by the small loans companies-charges that very often are higher than those made by our business firms in connection with goods they sell on an instalment basis.
In my judgment the banks have not done all they might in this field. As was demonstrated in evidence before the banking and commerce committee last year, the banks could do much more by way of expanding their small loans departments; and I suggest the government might take certain action to encourage the banks to expand and to cultivate their small loans business. As to why the banks have not been expanding their small loans departments, I suppose it is the easiest thing in the world for them not to do so because much of that business, as it now

Small Loans Act
exists, goes through the small loans companies; and they in turn-and this is shown by the statistics-obtain a good deal of their credit from the banks.
So the banks have the business anyway. They lend the money to the small loans companies, and the small loans companies in turn lend the money out to the ultimate borrowers. Evidence before the banking and commerce committee last year showed that the banks had in loans outstanding to small loans companies the sum of $29,500,000.
I know the argument is going to be made- and it is one of the strong arguments that might be advanced, unless it can be successfully answered-against this bill that if you bring down interest rates, laudable as that objective is, you are going to turn a lot of people who previously could obtain money from small loans companies to the loan sharks, and instead of getting money at 24 per cent a year they will have to pay 50 per cent a year or even more.
I do not think that is a necessary alternative at all. If such a lowering of interest rates may encourage the loan sharks, the government should not let such a fact-if it is a fact, and I do not admit that it is-stop them from passing this bill, because the thing the government needs to do is to take whatever action may be necessary, by passing this and other measures, so that people who are now getting money from small loans companies at 24 per cent will be able to get money at a much lower rate of interest.

I am coming to those steps. The legislation which the government has on the statute books today in other fields shows the kind of steps that need to be taken. The National Housing Act is a special act of this parliament with special provisions as far as bank lending is concerned. It encourages the banks to make money available to home owners. I am sure the parliamentary assistant will agree with me that had it not been for the National Housing Act, had it not been for the amendments to the Bank Act that the banks were not asking for-in fact, in some instances were rather reluctant to accept-we would not have the valuable contribution that this legislation is making to our Canadian economy.
Something on which I can speak with greater authority is the success of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Under that act almost any farmer

perhaps 95 per cent of the farmers of Canada-can go to the bank and obtain money, if he asks for it, for the purchase of farm machinery, for the remodelling of the farm home, for the installation of
[Mr. Argue.!
electricity, for the buying of better cattle, for the purchase of good seed, almost anything that will improve the farm as an operating unit, or improve his home, at an interest rate of 5 per cent.
Mr. 3enidickson: On the security of the farm.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Oh, no, not on the security of the farm; on the security of the machine that is purchased, that is all, and the personal reputation and honesty of the farmer who goes into the bank to do business. But as far as the bank is concerned there is a further guarantee from the government. The government and the people of Canada will stand behind those loans to the extent of 10 per cent of the aggregate amount of the loans in case of loss. What has happened? Has it cost the federal government tremendous sums of money? It has cost the federal government practically nothing. I suggest that without this legislation the farmers of Canada would be facing the same interest rates that are now charged by small loans companies.
The government's guarantee under the Farm Improvement Loans Act has been in effect for quite a number of years. A great deal of money has been lent under the legislation. The number of loans since 1945 have totalled 415,000, amounting to $451 million. The government has had to pay to the banks on account of losses the relatively tiny sum of $92,000 on just 175 claims. Someone behind me reminds me that they are still collecting some of that money, so even that loss on the loans covered may subsequently be reduced.
What is the cost to the government in the aggregate loss, compared with the amount of the loans? It is -02 per cent, or 1/500 part of the original government guarantee of 10 per cent of the aggregate amount of the loans. I suggest that without such a guarantee, which has cost the public of Canada over this long period of time much less than $100,000, the farmers of Canada would have had to pay many millions more in interest charges than they have had to pay because of this legislation.
Therefore I suggest to the government that they bring in another act-and they might call it the family welfare improvement act, an act to encourage banks to expand the legitimate small loans business that some of them are now providing-designed to make available to Canadian consumers generally the kind of credit at a reasonable rate of interest on which they are now forced to pay interest charges of 24 per cent a year.
MAY e, 1955
I am one who has great faith in the honesty and integrity of the vast majority of Canadian people. I believe that if such an act were backed by a guarantee by the federal government, perhaps similar to the guarantee under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the experience would be precisely the same, namely that the loss the government would have to pay would be very insignificant indeed. Such an act would provide great assistance to-and I repeat-the majority of families in this country who today are buying on the instalment plan or buying on credit through the small loans companies.
Since I have proposed this legislation I have been surprised to find out just how many people and how many households of this country buy on the instalment plan. I know many instances of men who may be earning such high salaries as $6,000, $8,000, $10,000 or more a year who are buying goods on the instalment plan. In many instances people who one would expect to know precisely the rate of interest they are paying are not aware of it until it is pointed out to them wdiat a tremendous rate of interest they really are paying.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: He pays his taxes on the instalment plan.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
That may be so. Because the need is so great and the cost to the government would be so small, I am suggesting that not only should they pass such an act, but they should bring in legislation that would provide a satisfactory alternative method of obtaining credit at a maximum rate of 12 per cent-yes, I would say that should be the very maximum-and if possible steps should be taken to get the interest rates reduced even further.
I know the argument is going to be made that the small loans companies have a lot of losses and they must have a huge interest rate in order to pay those losses. It will be claimed that there are so many dishonest Canadians, you know, and they have to repossess things and lose money. Well the small loans companies lose practically nothing. The main company in the small loans business in Canada makes the boast- and I am glad that they can make it-that they have yet to make their first repossession.
A table placed before the banking and commerce committee last year shows that for the period ending December 31, 1952, the reserve for bad debts of small loans companies, out of a total interest charged by those companies of 23-42 per cent, amounted to -26 per cent. So one-quarter of 1 per cent is all that the small loans companies have 5043.3-224*
Small Loans Act
set aside for that purpose. But their operating profit was 9-35 per cent, a very neat profit. It stands as a blot on our nation, when you think of the hard-working people who are pennypinching to pay this exorbitant interest rate so the small loans companies before our banking and commerce committee can set forth the fact that their operating profit before income tax amounted to 9-35 per cent.
At the same time there was placed on the record a table of the operational costs of the Canadian Bank of Commerce small loans department. That has done and is doing a relatively good service for the Canadian people. They were able to make the same kind of small loans in the same field, not at a total interest rate of 23-42 per cent but at 10-43 per cent. They were able to show, after having taken all the losses-which were small -that they had concluded the year with a satisfactory operating profit of 2-48 per cent on the business involved.
I can tell you why the Canadian Bank of Commerce are able to do as well as they have done in this field. It is because they are more efficient than small loans companies. The salaries of the Canadian Bank of Commerce department amounted to 2-81 per cent; those of the four loans companies amounted to 5-68 per cent. So the small loans companies have to have another 2-87 per cent for salaries. For advertising the Canadian Bank of Commerce spent -03 per cent; the small loans companies spent 1-19 per cent. That is the cost of their high pressure advertising; they drag in as many people as possible in order to give them loans at 24 per cent per year. The cost of funds to the Canadian Bank of Commerce was 2-09 per cent; the cost of funds to the small loans companies was 3-07 per cent. That is another place where a saving of -98 per cent could be made.
Of course the field of operating profit is where the largest saving could be made, a saving of 6-87 per cent. If you add up just those few savings I have mentioned-and I have not added the large item called "expenses" and some other items-you find that in this field there could easily be a saving of 11-88 per cent, which would bring the cost of loans down from 23-42 to 11-54 per cent.
The reason the rates are high is that these people make exorbitant profits and spend large sums of money in high pressure advertising in order to get the business through their doors. So I am suggesting to the government that the passage of this bill would not mean, and should not mean, that the Canadian consumer will be placed at the

Small Loans Act
mercy of loan sharks. Last year the government took a step in the right direction by making it possible for banks to accept chattel mortgages as security for moneys they loaned through their small loans departments. The government has already taken a good step by amending the Bank Act to raise the maximum ceiling on these loans to $3,500.
I suggest to the government that they should not stop there, and that once and for all they should get rid of this exorbitant rate of 24 per cent by at least cutting it in half. I do not think any loan company in Canada is worthy of being in the business if it cannot make a reasonable profit at 12 per cent. If it has to get out of the business because it is so inefficient, let it go; good-bye and good riddance. Let the government amend the Bank Act and bring in legislation such as I have suggested, which will give the Canadian people a satisfactory alternative whereby they can get loans at reasonable interest.
When I move my other bill, I intend to go into the even higher rates of interest which are currently being charged in Canada, not by the merchant who operates a small business but by Canada's largest and best known retail firms.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find some difficulty in speaking after my hon. friend from Assiniboia. I think many of us are finding difficulty in following my hon. friend, because he is usually so efficient and thoroughly covers the matter at hand. My particular interest at this moment, since he has covered the essentials in regard to the rate of interest, is in the methods of advertising that these people practise. We had some discussion not very long ago about the deceptive packaging of bacon, and I was glad that the government took some action in the matter. I can see now the results of that action.
I think the government should take some action too-and I thought it would have been a good idea if my hon. friend from Assiniboia had written into his bill something to that effect-which would prohibit the type of deceptive advertising used by certain vampires of the small loans business. This matter is brought to my attention at the moment by an item in my own local newspaper, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of April 22, 1955, which I quote:
The Co-operative Union of Canada decided in convention Thursday to make representation to the federal government to require finance companies and business organizations to declare to the borrower or the instalment purchaser a total yearly-
The emphasis is mine on the word "yearly". -rate of interest being levied in each transaction. Delegates claimed that the existing practice of

interest charging by the month on small loans and on instalment purchase financing by some companies did not disclose to the borrower or the purchaser the true rate of interest.
There is a footnote, which says:
The Co-operative Union of Canada represents 860 local co-ops and 770,000 members.
As an example of the particular type of thing I mean, I think I might say, without making any derogatory remarks about anybody, that the people who avail themselves of these small loans, or a great many of them, are not accustomed to business methods and business practices. Some of them are rather easy to deceive in that particular matter.
Let me give an example of the type of notice which is very common in our newspapers. Let us assume that we are going to make a loan of $100. We see the advertisement saying "You get $100. You pay at the end of the first month only $9. At the end of the second month you pay only $9." So it goes on down the line till at the end of 12 months you discover-and the advertising emphasizes the word "only" you have only paid $108. Victims of this system have said to me, "That is not an exorbitant rate of interest; that is only 8 per cent". Of course we all know better than that. We know that the borrower has not the use of the $100 for the 12 months. He has the use of the $100 for only one month. Then when you get down to six months he has the use of only half that amount, and so on until you get down to the final month when he discovers-or he does not discover, in many cases-that for the use of one-twelfth of the principal which he has borrowed he is paying exactly the same charge as he paid during the first month. That is what I mean by deceptive advertising, and there is a great deal of it. There are many different types of that same deceptive advertising. The trouble is, of course, that these borrowers do not realize that the principal in their hands has been steadily decreasing while the interest payment is maintained and is constant.
As to the general or larger question which was dealt with by my hon. friend, I agree with him that the government has some responsibility in this matter. I agree that the government should accept some blame for what certain loan sharks are doing. These people are running a perfectly legal and often respectable business, but some of the people I know who have borrowed money from them have been extremely sorry they did so. They are little people, those who least of all can afford to indulge in the luxury of obtaining a loan of that kind. I think the government has some responsibility,

in that since 1939 it has been possible for these interest rates which have been pointed out by my hon. friend to be collected legally, by virtue of an act which allows up to 24 per cent per annum-I think that is the rate-to be charged.
One answer, of course, that one might get to this argument is that these people are fundamentally a poor risk, and that the rate therefore must be extremely high in order to compensate the companies for the losses sustained. Statistics give the lie to that argument. My colleague said that the amount lost amounted to twenty-six one-hundredths of 1 per cent of the yield of the loans. I think he should have stated that this is the amount of the reserve which was set aside by these companies. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the reserve which these companies set aside, on the average and over the years, would be more than the actual loss which it is meant to cover.
Of course, the free enterprise people would say that if these people do not want this type of loan they are not obliged to obtain it. However, may I say that the human element enters into all these things. We have people who need money because of sickness, accident, or the death, if you like, of some one of their relatives; and may I mention death particularly because for most people it is an expensive business to die these days. I suggest that these borrowers get into difficulty. They do not know in what direction to turn. Then suddenly along comes someone who says, "We will give you some money on your own note of hand, no questions asked" and all the rest of it. Of necessity they fall for that type of propaganda.
This business of caveat emptor-let the buyer beware-is part of the law of the jungle. In these enlightened days I suggest that governments should assume some responsibility for the protection of people who do not know how to protect themselves. People who are qualified financially have no difficulty in getting money at reasonable rates-I would say the average is perhaps 6 per cent-from the banks. The banks can now operate small loans departments. They do so at an effective rate of interest about half that which the loan companies charge. Why cannot these latter companies operate at the same rate as that at which the banks operate? That is a question I cannot answer.
This small loans business, as I said, may have assumed an air of respectability, but I do not think that fact makes it any less dangerous. Of course we no longer have the situation prevailing where a woman on Monday morning wraps the clock in her shawl and takes it down to the pawnshop; but I suggest than when she took the clock down
Small Loans Act
to the pawnshop she obtained just as good a deal as she does when she approaches some of these financial advisers, with their plush offices by day and their neon lights by night attracting you in there so that you may borrow some money and be rooked just to that much greater an extent. They call themselves financial consultants, forsooth; and they invite you in to have your many little debts consolidated, in order to get them all in the same place; "the same place", of course, being your name on a note in their office.
The advertisements are screaming at these potential borrowers all the time. All day they are screaming at them to come in and borrow money on their own note of hand, without security. They offer advice by which these people can be induced to borrow money. I do not know whether or not my friend gave the figures, but I obtained them. According to those figures 70 per cent of these people do labouring work, artisans, people working in offices doing clerical and other non-manual work. In other words, they are the poorer-paid people of the country.
I think they should have protection at least to the extent recommended by my hon. friend, and that the interest rate should be reduced from its present legal maximum of 24 per cent to a maximum of 12 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) I think I should say something in reply to the sponsor of this bill.
The Small Loans Act, which was enacted in 1939, resulted largely from the work of the parliamentary committees. This whole problem is something in which members of parliament have taken a good deal of interest. The problem received a great amount of study by the banking and commerce committees in the sessions of 1937 and 1938. This attention was given to the matter because, prior to that time, the banking and commerce committee was being asked to review regularly petitions for the incorporation of a number of individual companies in this field.
There was a great deal of evidence showing that, without regulation and government supervision, some extremely unfortunate circumstances had developed and that a very high rate of interest-much higher than that described by my hon. friend-was being charged in many instances.
As a result of the deliberations of that committee, it is true that a maximum

Small Loans Act
monthly flat rate of 2 per cent for small loans was recommended. Admittedly this rate was considered to be experimental. However, before these committees evidence was taken from representatives in the field in the United States. The parliamentarians had a great deal of experience, as I say, as a result of hearing applications for incorporation of individual companies. This maximum rate of 2 per cent was set, and it has been in existence since 1939.
In 1946 the government introduced an amendment to this act. It was then proposed to reduce the rate to 1J per cent per month. This bill received second reading in the House of Commons and was referred to the banking and commerce committee which gave it some study, but the bill itself was not reported.
It happened that at about this time, between 1945 to 1948, the largest lenders in this small personal loan field had in fact reduced their general rate to borrowers to It per cent. However, about this same time the general costs of doing business in any field were on the rise. In 1948 the lenders generally returned to a rate of about 1| per cent. Since 1950 the general rate, according to the reports that are filed, works out again at about 2 per cent.
I am sure hon. members will be interested in the experience of other countries. As I say, when our legislation was enacted in 1939 and prior thereto, considerable evidence was available as to the experience in the United States. In that country legislation in this field is within the jurisdiction of the states rather than the federal government, so practices and rates vary. However, the maximum rate in most of the states of the United States for loans in this field is 3 per cent per month, and there the ceiling under which the law applies, generally speaking, is even less than ours, being $300 rather than $500.
In Great Britain I understand that at the present time there is no statutory maximum interest rate but the courts place the onus on the borrower to prove that the rate being charged is unfair if the rate is less than 4 per cent per month, and if the rate is more than 4 per cent per month the onus is on the lender to establish that the rate is not unfair.
The main purpose of this small loans legislation is to ensure that lending facilities are available to necessitous persons who have need for small sums of money and are not able to get them from sources used by others. That is why there is a ceiling. At the present time the ceiling is $500. I could not tell from my hon. friend's remarks whether he entirely understood that the

Small Loans Act has no application whatever to time sales of goods. It does not apply to conditional sales agreements, hire-purchase agreements and so on, to which he did make some reference. I assume he did so by way of reference to the other bill he has on the order paper to amend the Interest Act, which would have a bearing in that type of business.
We are discussing in this bill the application for a loan on a personal note without the element of a business transaction. Experience has shown that only by strict regulation and by providing an adequate rate is it likely that the public will be protected against excessive rates. This was the evidence before the banking and commerce committee in 1937 and 1938. If the maximum rate is too low the result is simply that regulated loans dry up; and it was established, in the opinion of the parliamentary committee, that the loan sharks would be the alternative and would enter the field.
I should like to read to the house a few extracts from the report of the banking and commerce committee of 1938 on this point. At page 424 of that report this was said:
Obviously the state can intervene over rates only within a limited field; for naturally a legislative rate at which money is not obtainable is of doubtful benefit to necessitous people. In the debates over the subject it would almost seem to have been at times forgotten that to legislate a maximum rate is an injunction that, if people cannot borrow at the prescribed rate, they cannot borrow at all.
Again, at page 425 the committee report had this to say:
The rates of the several states-*
Of the United States.
-were presumably established after exhaustive inquiry and, in several instances, after the legislative prescription of lower rates had led to a diminution in the supply of licensed credit with a return of bootlegged loans in volume.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. May I adjourn the debate?

speechtext:
This is the item I have been waiting for, and I think the minister has as well, because we want to discuss the problem of immigration. However, I do not propose to take too much time. I have been raising the question of the general policy with regard to immigration for the last three years in the hope that I could get an answer from the minister. I was not able to get one from the present minister's predecessor, so I raise the question now for the minister's benefit.
Earlier this year I drew attention to this problem. I am interested in the racial groupings within the country, and I am interested in knowing what is the policy of the government with regard to retaining the racial groupings we have had in this country from the early days. On other occasions I have pointed out that the percentage of people who trace their origin to the British Isles has been declining. I have drawn the attention of the house to the fact that in the days of the great immigration into this country, in the first few years of this century, 60 per cent of the immigration came from the British Isles. Over the first 50 years of this century, 50 per cent of the total number of immigrants entering Canada came from the British Isles.
I point out that I am not thinking of excluding anyone; I am not talking as an exclusionist. There was no exclusion of people of various racial origins in the days of the great migration to this country in the first few years of this century. Yet at that time 60 per cent of the immigrants were from the British Isles. Similarly, I suggest no exclusion now. If we are to have an immigration policy at all and want to attract people to this country, we naturally want to

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration get them from as many places as we can suitably obtain them. I am not objecting to the present policy of the department or its extensive attempts to gain immigrants from the various countries of the world. We have many racial groups represented in Canada, but it is still our duty to look to the future.
Are we, through lack of care or lack of success in attracting immigrants from the British Isles, creating a trend whereby in the course of time the racial groupings within this country will be materially altered? I raise the question, but I do not myself say it should be necessary for the government to use any policy to alter the basic racial divisions within this country from what they were 50 years ago or even 20 years ago.

Some point was also made in the estimates committee about the possibility of lending money to the dependents of immigrants for assisted passage. If I could persuade myself that this would really stimulate immigration from the British Isles I would be very happy indeed to recommend to my colleagues that we extend the scheme to the dependents of immigrants; but our experience has been- at least I would say we have deduced from our experience-that in the kind of full employment and the kind of prosperity we have had in this country in recent years, it has taken the immigrant himself such a relatively short time to accumulate enough money to bring his family-and moreover he could pay for their passage in sterling- that there would not have been very much advantage, except for impecunious people, to have loans of this sort, and in many cases even they did not seem to have been much deterred by this difficulty; but I am still quite open to conviction on that point.

I want to see more immigration from the United Kingdom. I would not want anyone to misunderstand my position on that; but fortunately or unfortunately-perhaps I should not use the word "unfortunately"- we cannot conscript people in the United Kingdom to come here. Although it might appeal to some people as being simply providence to ask for more money than you expect to spend, in other words to leave some room to turn around, there is another aspect to the matter in public finance which is very important. This motion may be more by way of token than of great consequence to the budget, but I suggest that it is worth consideration on this ground. One or two aspects of the administration of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration that came out in the committee proceedings deserve attention, in


my opinion, at this time. They have to do with the relationship of this department to two other departments. I think this item is perhaps the appropriate one on which to make the point I have in mind.
What we are doing, of course, is voting funds to enable this department to carry on its administration. In doing that I think we should look first at the purpose of the department and, in the second place, the efficiency and economy of its administration. In this item No. 67 provision is made for field and inspectional services. Coming under that provision are 139 special officers whose function is to do the same kind of work as that done by the national employment service of the Department of Labour. That is the first point I want to make. I wish to point out that here we have two departments doing the same job.
What is that job? It is to advise immigrants as to labour conditions in Canada, the work that is available, the opportunities for employment and for farming or business which are available in this country. When we have set up under the Department of Labour a nation-wide system of employment counsel covering every part of Canada and presumably familiar with work conditions and opportunities in every part of Canada, one would think that service would be the appropriate one to supply information to intending immigrants.
It is true that this information must be supplied in their own countries. Therefore I suppose the information which these officers collect must be sent abroad to be delivered to the prospective immigrants in their own countries. But why should this department of immigration have 139 officers in Canada going about the country collecting information which, it seems to me, already is or should be available in the Department of Labour? That is the first conflict between departments that I think deserves the consideration of the government.
Let me point out this fact. In Canada itself we have the labour department and the citizenship and immigration department both collecting this information, whereas abroad we have the immigration department using the information by delivering it to the immigrants.
The other administrative question is the relationship of this department to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Although this department chooses to have its own employment officers, it does not choose to have its own doctors. There is nothing in the vote here to provide for medical inspection of immigrants abroad. That provision appears in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.

On referring to the appropriate place in the estimates, Mr. Chairman, you will find that some 315 personnel are to be supplied for immigration purposes by the Department of National Health and Welfare at a cost of $1,151,000, which is properly a part of the expenses of the department of immigration. Purely as an administrative and accounting problem, and as a matter of efficiency, I suggest that the government review this separation of services.
I suggest that the duplication should be reviewed from another viewpoint because, with two departments responsible, the tendency is for neither to take the full responsibility. There is the possibility that you will find the unfortunate immigrant, in places like Toronto or Montreal, being sent from the department of immigration to the Department of Labour in order to find a job, and then being sent back from the Department of Labour to the department of immigration because they both have some responsibility and each can pass the buck to the other. Hence for more reasons than one I suggest that this problem should be reviewed with the idea in mind of putting the labour counselling service under one department and coordinating it in that place.
The question of the productivity of the department is not an easy one to deal with. One can only compare the number on the staff and the number of immigrants brought in. That is a mathematical comparison, and perhaps it does not mean a great deal. Actually the figures the minister gave indicate that five years ago the department was staffed with 2,913 civil servants, after making some adjustments and including Indian affairs which have nothing to do with immigration, compared with a total at the present time of 3,954, or an increase of 1,041 in the staff of the department in five years. That is an increase of more than one-third. In the same period the number of immigrants admitted to the country has not shown the corresponding variation. I believe 1950 was a relatively small year but in 1951, the year of heaviest immigration since the war, 190,000 or more people came to Canada, compared with
154,000	in the last calendar year, 1954.
As I say, I do not put too much weight on these figures because I feel that the problem of the immigration department is probably more difficult today than it was immediately after the war, and is getting more difficult all the time. As has already been said, the great opportunity to get immigrants from the United Kingdom was immediately after the war. At that time would-be immigrants were lined up for six blocks in front of the Liverpool office waiting to come to Canada. The
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration problem then was transportation. The house is aware of the steps taken by the government of Ontario at that time to provide air transportation, but because the problem of transportation was not adequately met at the time by this department that opportunity was allowed to pass. Today we have not the same scope in securing the immigrants we want in this country.
I believe it is a fallacy today to expect immigrants to drop into our lap. They are not hanging in the trees any more, and we have to go after the kind of immigration that meets the requirements of the country. I do not place too much emphasis on the figures, and I do not intend by what I say to try to restrict the department in its expenditures because I feel the problem is more difficult now than it was and that every effort should be made to go to the places where suitable immigrants are available and get them to come here.
We have been lucky in many respects. We have had a good many from the Scandinavian countries, but such immigrants are not now available. We were fortunate in the immigration of the displaced persons. We got very fine immigrants, among them professional people whose training would cost a great deal if it had to be duplicated in this country. A great many people came here who were able to establish their own businesses, and we were fortunate in securing them. We were fortunate in getting the Dutch farmers who came here. They were a fine lot. But these sources are drying up, and we have to work a little harder now. It is only in the spirit of promoting efficient administration that I point out these problems of overlapping and separation of function which have been discovered in the course of the examination of these estimates in the special committee on estimates.

I hope none of it is spent, and if none of it is spent I do not think it will be a case of overtaxing the Canadian people.
