speechtext:
There are a number of questions that arise in connection with this general section, Mr. Chairman, on which I wish to secure from the minister the opinion of his department.
The first has to do with the liability of the Indian for income taxes. One does not have to go back very far-it was toward the latter days of the first great war-to find when income taxes were introduced into the law of this country. It was believed at that time that it was a temporary measure that would be abolished as soon as the war was over. Indeed, that fiction has been carried on pretty well ever since by referring to the act as the Income War Tax Act.
However, in recent years, and certainly I think within the last year or so, the department administering the income tax has been
3552	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration imposing that tax upon Indians in respect of income which was earned outside the reserve, or in respect of any transactions executed beyond the confines of the reserve.
This has been a cause of great alarm, if not indignation, amongst the Indians. They claim, and I think rightly, that under the law, tradition and history and the treaties of the past indicate that at no time was the Indian to be subject to taxation. This was the principle back in 1763, with the royal proclamation of that year, and it was followed year by year after the establishment of responsible government in Canada until very recently.
The fiction upon which it is founded is this. We pay the Indian treaty money in recognition of the fact that he owned this country and still exercises an ownership over it, and that the government, representing the crown, is required to pay a yearly amount in ransom in compensation to the Indians for their rights and in recognition of the sovereignty they at one time enjoyed.
The Indian today is very much aroused over the imposition of income tax upon him, under the circumstances to which I have alluded. The halcyon days of no income tax upon other citizens of Canada have disappeared, but the Indian contends that there is no legal justification for the imposition of income tax upon him. Indeed, representations have been made from time to time by the chiefs to the Indian affairs branch, and the indignation of the chiefs has been intensified by the fact that at no time have successive ministers of Indian affairs been able to point out to them the legal justification for what is being done.
My information from the grand council of the North American Indian brotherhood is that two conferences under the Indian Act took place under my hon. friend's predecessor in office, but that on neither occasion was the minister able to place before the Indians the constitutional authority upon which this taxation is based.
I have the Indian Act before me, and I am familiar with the interpretation that has been placed thereon. I ask the minister if he will explain to the Indians, as clearly as he can, the legal justification in this instance, having regard to the original proclamation that was made immediately after the cessation of French rule in America, and the subsequent treaties. Will he explain how it is that his department has not had a submission made to the courts for the purpose of determining this matter once and for all? If there is liability then let the minister, representing the Indians, make a submission to the courts to determine the question; and if the supreme


court of this country comes to the conclusion that the law does permit the imposition of income tax on the Indian, that will be the end of it. But I believe that so long as the income tax is imposed there will be considerable ill feeling and remonstrance among the tribes.
I am sure another chief, who is sitting in the house at the moment-I am referring to the Minister of Agriculture who, I believe, was honoured a few years ago as Chief Thunderchild-will have received representations-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: I am sure the minister has no exemption from income tax.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: Oh, he is only honorary; and I am only honorary, too. For that reason the rights that flow from proclamations and subsequent treaties do not apply to us. All we have are the prerogatives and privileges, but none of the rights.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: And the feathers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
And we do not receive the payment of treaty moneys from year to year.
I suggest in all seriousness that the minister could deal with this subject, which is of greatest concern to the Indians, by the simple procedure of having this question submitted by the Minister of Justice and the law officers of the crown for the consideration and determination of the supreme court.
Then I return once again to a matter that has aroused intense indignation among the Indians. I refer to the use that has been made by the department of section 9 of the Indian Act. This has to do with the preparation of the band list, on the basis of which the question of membership in the band is determined and decided. Section 9 reads as follows:
Within six months after a list has been posted in accordance with section 8 or within three months after the name of a person has been added to or deleted from a band list . . . may, by notice in writing to the registrar, containing a brief statement of the grounds therefor, protest the inclusion, omission, addition, or deletion, as the case may be, of the name of that person.
Then subsection 2 says:
Where a protest is made to the registrar under this section he shall cause an investigation to be made into the matter-
And so on. Quite a number of investigations have been made. The result has been that Indian has been set against Indian within the band membership. A vast amount of ill feeling has been aroused. Gossip and hearsay have taken the place of legal evidence to determine whether or not given individuals

have the right to be on the list, because of the fact that somewhere in the past white blood found its way into the veins of some ancestors.
The result has been a great degree of ill feeling engendered and a belief that unfairness is being done. These cases of unfairness are apparent in the incongruous definitions of what is a white and what is an Indian. I am not going into the particulars of those paradoxical conclusions and decisions, but it is very difficult to understand why a half-blood becomes a white or an Indian, depending upon whether or not the Indian blood is either maternally or paternally inherited.
A large number of investigations have taken place, and I am not going to review those cases except to say that I know of no decisions that have been handed down by the registrar.
I hope no decisions are handed down. I hope this species of emasculated court will not be permitted by the minister to dignify its conclusions as judgments determining the rights of individuals. I hope the minister will find a way whereby, without in any way eluding or circumventing the law, a state of affairs can be brought about which will remove this serious source of grievance.
I have known Indians over the years, since the earliest days in the prairie provinces, going back to the days of Gabriel Dumont, who returned to the area which is now Saskatchewan; I have known of the Indians of the territorial days. They are a people who are intensely loyal, and a people whose patriotic services in two world wars have been beyond words of commendation. They have the right to ask that every consideration be given to their feelings. In this regard they are aroused. They feel that something in the nature of tyrannical administration, affecting their rights and in some cases casting doubt on their ancestry, has been introduced into the law by section 9.
Will the minister not give consideration to obliterating what has been done, or at least assuring us that what has been done will not be continued in the future and that what commissions have been appointed will not render final decisions? I think fairness, justice and equity would be assured if a simple, retroactive declaration were made by law, that those who were resident in the bands several years ago shall be considered to have been regularly constituted members of the bands, thereby putting their descendants in the same position. Something of that kind would certainly bring about a condition under which many cases of injustice, as the Indians see it, would be avoided.
I make this appeal to the minister because I know that since he has taken over his
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration portfolio there has been nothing in the nature of any decision by the registrar. Nothing has been done beyond the hearings by the commissions. For all that he deserves the thanks of the Indians, and I am sure he will receive them. But I do ask him to go one step further and give these people the assurance that their rights will not be subject to periodic challenge based on hearsay and suspicion. One just has to read the evidence given at these commissions-I dignify it by the name of evidence, because I have no other word that would apply; "testimony" might be more applicable-to learn that witnesses come along and give evidence to this effect. They say their grandmother allegedly told somebody else that a third party had a doubtful ancestry.
Well, that kind of thing may be the only testimony available; but when there is the incentive to exaggerate the evidence because of the fact that the more who are removed by such evidence the fewer there will be in the band, and the fewer in the band the more money there will be to distribute, one can understand the forces that motivate the giving of that type of hearsay evidence.
I ask the minister to give reconsideration to this matter, for I have never known the Indians on the western plains to be more aroused than they are at the present time. They are aroused at what they believe to be an injustice, the basis of which they cannot understand. They do not realize the purpose. of the commissions nor the ends to be attained.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
I am hoping that because a committee has been set up to study the estimates we shall not do away entirely with the discussion of a problem as serious as our Indian problem in Canada. I have several thousand Indians in my constituency who are living under deplorable conditions. It is true that conditions have improved a little. I hope the improvement will continue more rapidly.
There has been no discussion of the Indian problem on the floor of the house during this session. At the last session there was very little. During the years of the twentieth parliament a committee was established, composed of a lot of very fine gentlemen and one lady senator. They studied this problem at great length. There was a lot of discussion, and the people of Canada and the members of the House of Commons generally realized that it was a major problem. The Indian Act was revised, and steps were taken to make a start on making conditions easier for the Indians and teaching them a new way of life.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
First I want to say I am not on my feet tonight to make carping criticism of the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. When the present Minister of Finance took over this department he showed a great deal of interest. He gave this problem a great deal of thought. Indians came in and talked to him on many occasions. I will say this for the minister; he won the confidence of the Indians. Any minister who is to properly administer this department must first of all get the Indians to have confidence in him. I am hoping the present minister will do as good a job and be as thoughtful in dealing with the Indians as the present Minister of Finance when he was in that department.
One thing I have learned about the Indian is that he never forgets. If you do him a good turn he will remember it; but if you do him a bad turn, or if you speak hastily at times without giving consideration to what you are saying, you make an enemy instead of a friend.
I did not speak on Indian affairs last session because I had been out of the house for four years. I had lost contact with my Indian friends, and I was not in a position to know what had been done since the new act was proclaimed and the new thinking regarding the whole Indian problem had been adopted. Last summer I did make it my business to go to a number of reserves in my constituency. It was so muddy that I was not able to get to them all, but I found that quite an improvement had taken place.
When I was in the House of Commons in 1945, 1946 and 1947 I emphasized two things. The first was that we had to provide Indians with schools so they could get an education. Schools were built on all the reserves. Another thing I mentioned was the need of hospitals. We have a good hospital in our area that takes good care of the sick Indians. The second thing was housing. Houses have been built for a few of our older Indians.
By the way, the Indians in one particular reserve, the Thundercloud reserve, sent word and asked me to come up and see them. I went. I sent word of the day I would be there. When I got to where the road turned off the highway I 'was met by an Indian who guided me in to the reserve. I am sure if he had not been there to guide me I would not have been able to find my way through the potholes.
I was met and welcomed by the chief of the band. He held my hand for a long time and said, "I think I never see you again. You good friend." I think that repaid me for any little work I have done in connection with Indians. We had a long conference. Most
[Mr. Campbell.!
of the band were there, and a number of suggestions were made by the Indians, who asked me to bring their case before this House of Commons. That is why I am on my feet tonight.
One of the first things I asked them to do was take me to some of the houses in which they were living. Mr. Chairman, I wish all the members of this House of Commons and the people of Canada generally could see the type of houses in which the majority of these Indians are living and the conditions under which they are living. There would be no hesitation whatsoever in giving all the assistance possible to the Indian affairs branch and the minister who is administering that department to make things different, although there have been a few houses built for the older Indians.
Here we have people who for generations had a whole country from which to get their living. Whenever they got hungry they could go out and kill buffalo, deer or antelope, and provide themselves with plenty of food. They could make a shelter, and they could get their clothing from the skins of those animals. Those days are completely gone. The older generation that got its livelihood in that way are completely lost. They do not know how to do any of the kinds of work the white man requests of them. They have absolutely no way of making a living. If it were not for the fact that we have family allowances, and that the old Indians are now getting old age pensions, the Indian affairs branch would either have to feed all those people or let them starve to death; one or the other.
I looked at a number of these houses lived in by the majority of whom I am talking. What kind of houses do they live in? They have gathered a few logs-and not very good logs-they have a wall six or seven feet high, and they have put on an earth roof on which there is very little pitch. Last summer it rained almost continuously for weeks, and for days on end water poured through those roofs on to the people who were in those shacks. I want to warn the department here that if something is not done soon, at least to get roofs that will shelter these people from rain, we are going to have a recurrence of tuberculosis. Neither an Indian nor anybody else can live in that kind of housing and be free from tuberculosis and many other diseases.
I find that this has taken place during the last few years. As I said earlier we have had day schools on these reserves for the last three years. Now we have a generation of boys and girls between 16 and 19 years of age coming out of school who can read and

write but cannot do very much else. In the -village where I live we are not far from three different reserves. In the last two or three falls dozens of young men have come into our district looking for work. What kind of work can they do? They cannot do any work. They do not really know how to do anything. There are jobs. There is a scarcity of farm labour in my constituency, and in my district particularly.
The white farmers do not hire these boys. Why? Because they cannot drive a truck, they cannot handle a combine, they cannot handle a tractor. Today we have mechanized farming, and unless these young men have some kind of training in operating these machines I do not know what is going to become of them. They are going to become a charge on our people. They are going to become a group of tramps. I think something should be done to provide these boys with some kind of help to learn how to do things.
I had a conference with some of the officials of the department yesterday or the day before, and I made the suggestion that some kind of technical training should be given these boys. I am not proposing that the government or the department set up a large technical training scheme. I do not think it would be practical and I do not think it would work. It would be costly, and it might be a complete failure. But I do think that the department could have a few mobile units- a van with a mechanic and a carpenter- which would spend perhaps two or three weeks on each reserve and then move on. We could see next year what progress they had made.
As I have stated, these Indians need homes. That is one of the first things they need. They have no idea how to set about building a wooden house. If they could get some training so that even a few of them could get started, it would be of great benefit. It does not take a very clever carpenter to build a house. Nearly anybody with average intelligence, after working with a carpenter for a few weeks, could learn how to build a house. A mechanic could give some basic training in practical mechanical matters.
Some of the reserves are getting a few tractors, and a few of the Indians on these reserves are getting a small number of old trucks. I have not seen any good trucks; I have seen a number of trucks which are barely hanging together as I passed through on the road. When the trucks broke down they were not able to repair them. One of the reasons these trucks broke down is that these people did not know how to operate them or
6, 1955
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration take care of them. That is a suggestion. I think that some practical beginning has to be made along these lines.
I do not know what they are going to do about the girls. The girls are in this position, that they are leaving home. When they come out of school a few of them have been taken into the Indian hospital in North Battleford and have received training. Some of them have lived in the hospital for two or three years. They have learned how to cook with an electric stove, and they have had frigi-daires. They have had nice rooms and clean beds and have been well dressed. They meet young Indians and decide to get married. Then you are up against a serious problem. When they get married they just go back to the reserve and live in one of these shacks.
The day I was on one of the reserves there was a very clean, well dressed, nice looking girl. She had spent three or four years in the hospital and had that training, and she had married an Indian and gone back to one of these houses, about which I am talking, to live with the parents. There is not much hope for the girls, as far as I can see, until we get the boys trained so they can earn a living and are able to build a decent house to which to take their wives. This is a problem to which I have given much thought and about which I have been very much concerned.
When I was reading the reports of the estimates committee, in report No. 14, at page 413, I found a statement that made me feel badly. This was a statement by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. The committee were discussing housing, and the item in question was to provide a sum of money to build houses for these Indians who could not afford to pay for them themselves. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre said:
I should like to make it clear that I think it is fine to build these houses if you are going to try to make the Indian pay it back over a period of years, like any other citizen, but for the life of me I cannot understand why we build homes for Indians-1 do not care how destitute they are- unless we try to get some of the money back.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I felt badly about that statement. I hope the hon. member did not really mean it. I hope there are no other members in the House of Commons who have the same idea. I want to make this promise to the minister. As far as I am concerned, and as far as this group are concerned, we will give him every encouragement not only to build houses but to do as much as possible for the Indians who are in the desperate condition most of us know about.
I want to cut short what I was going to say; nevertheless I want to make one or two
3556	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration more suggestions. One of the questions the Indians discussed with me was the difficulty they had in getting meat. I said to them, "Can you not get any deer, moose or anything like that?" They said, "The trouble with us is this. When the season is open for deer, while it is true there are deer in this country the white men come out by the hundreds, and we are afraid to go out in the bush while the white men are hunting. If you could just get the government to give us one day or perhaps two days so we could get some meat for ourselves, we would appreciate it. We do not hunt for sport. When we go out, we go in order to try to get some meat." I said, "That is a provincial matter, but I will draw it to the attention of the government and ask if they cannot make some arrangement with the provincial government to give the Indians that privilege."
Shortly after that discussion I came across an article in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of February 11, 1955, which illustrates this point clearly. It is headed "Disgraced" and it reads as follows:
Saskatchewan hunters must look upon the 1954 game bag with mixed emotions. True, they carried home more than one million ducks and more than 20,000 deer, as well as much other game. But they can scarcely be proud of the fact that 13 hunters died from wounds and that 39 others suffered nonfatal injuries. Such sombre statistics are indeed cause for reflection.
Other figures should cause not a few red faces. Apart from human and legitimate game targets, hunters' bullets found their marks in 19 cattle, three calves, six horses, one goat, several gasoline drums, a combine, a car and a truck. Some of the shots which did this damage were fired deliberately and _ criminally. Others were fired in thoughtless stupidity. Hunters must accept public ridicule for such acts and vow to reform, or they must accept the doubtful reputation of being anything but keen-eyed. As such they disgrace their prehistoric ancestors, who lived by taking careful and unerring aim.
Mr. Chairman, the committee has listened to me patiently. I know the minister is in a hurry to get through. I am therefore going to curtail my remarks. However, I want to assure the minister that even though I am sitting on the opposition benches, if there is anything I can do to help to solve this problem he can count on my support.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on this item. During the first two parliaments that I sat in this chamber I had many Indians in my constituency. Then there was a redistribution and I lost the Indians but I never seemed to lose contact with them.
Before I say the few words I wish to say, may I assure the minister that I do not rise with any animosity toward him, the department or anybody else. I am like the hon.


member for The Battlefords; if I can do anything at all to help in solving this Indian problem I shall be only too pleased to do it.
When the minister replies-and he does not need to do so until he is ready-I should like to know how many more houses have been built at Norway House since the last time I represented the constituency. I might assure the minister that I am going there this summer. I have made arrangements to go this summer to Cross Lake, and Norway House, when the house finishes its work. I should like to know about the hospital stations. I had some trouble getting to see them but I got there anyway, and I saw how they were working. I thought they were a credit to the department.
In about 1949 the department of Indian affairs sent four Indian nurses to New Zealand to be trained as midwives. What happened to them? Did they come back? Where are they working today, or have they gone into the ranks of the married? In the veterans affairs committee I asked questions about our Indian soldier settlers. I obtained the information that in Manitoba there are 78 such settlers. I should like to know from the minister what progress they have made. Have they their farms half paid for yet, or is the interest going to beat them? What is the situation there? The minister can either drop me a note and tell me about that matter or he can tell me when he is answering the other questions.
The hon. member for The Battlefords spoke about vocational training. I think that is a wonderful thing. My experience in the north country has been that when you teach the Indian something he does not forget it. He is also quick to learn. At Norway House there was a young Indian-I think he was about 18 or 19 years old-who could slab logs better than any white man I ever saw. Unfortunately that boy was drowned, but there will be more like him there.
I did some visiting in some of the houses there. In one of the houses I visited there were parts of two outboard motors lying around. I do not know how many pieces there were, but to me there looked to be about 30 or 40. I asked the young chap there what he was going to do with them. He said he was going to make one engine out of two. I served a good apprenticeship on the river Clyde, building boats, engines and so forth, and I thought he had quite a job in hand. But two days later I saw him coming up the Nelson river with the two engines made into one. He had done a wonderful job. I might tell you that the only tools he had were a pair of pliers and a soldering bolt.

I therefore say this. Do not have any hesitation about this vocational training. I do not know just how it can be done, but there must be plenty of brains in the Indian affairs department which can devise ways and means to bring this vocational training to these young men.
What has happened since we brought health services to the Indians? Let us go back to when I came to this house first in 1943. Conditions among the Indians then were deplorable. The death rate was very high on some of the reserves. That situation has been remedied by the services the Indian department has rendered, but you have a bigger problem on your hands now than you ever had before because the Indians are not dying in such numbers. There are gradually becoming more of them, and you have to face the problem whether you are going to make the Indians wards of the government for all time to come or whether you are going to put them on an equal basis with white men.
The Indians were the original settlers of this country, and I think we should try to get them straightened out before we have more Indians than white people. I want to ask the minister one more question. Why does Manitoba only get a grant of $250 for fairs while Alberta and Saskatchewan get more? I do not like to see Manitoba discriminated against in these matters. I am not going to take any more time, because maybe somebody else wants to say something.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: I have no desire to hold up the proceedings tonight. I have been deeply interested in all that has been said up to the present time. There is no doubt that most of the Indians are in a very deplorable situation economically and that they face a yet more deplorable situation if unemployment develops as it appears it is going to develop and they become unable to obtain the employment which they have been obtaining during the last few years. I ask hon. members to imagine the state they will be in. I thought I should like to have the minister give us some idea of what he has in mind in connection with the various problems which have been so well indicated by those who have already spoken. Could the minister talk to us a while about this matter?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
Before I attempt to do that, perhaps I might anticipate the hour and ask if the committee would give its indulgence for a very few minutes after ten o'clock. I am informed there is a real prospect of finishing if we could have that indulgence.
I shall make my remarks very brief. With respect to the specific questions asked by the hon. member for Selkirk, perhaps he would,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration as he rather indicated, let me give the answers on another occasion, because they involve a little research.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: Don't forget. That is all I ask.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS

Oh, I have a fair memory, and I can assure the hon. member for Selkirk that if there is one province-well, with one possible exception-I would not want to discriminate against, it is Manitoba.
I thought the remarks made by the hon. member for The Battlefords and the hon. member for Selkirk were most constructive. There is no doubt that the very excellent work done in recent years by the Department of National Health and Welfare in eradicating disease among the Indians and improving their general health has, as several hon. members have indicated, created a very serious problem.
The traditional way of life of many of the Indians, especially in the northern part of the country, cannot be pursued by all those who are growing up now. I feel pretty sure that education and the kind of housing which will make it possible for them to profit by education are, as the hon. member for The Battlefords indicated, the two real keys to this problem. We are deeply concerned about the problem of technical education and the best and most practical way of accomplishing it. I could continue at considerable length about this matter, and on another occasion I shall be very happy to do so, but perhaps just saying what I have said is almost enough.
In my view these are the two key things, and the more closely the education of the Indians is integrated with the education of the rest of the population the sooner the Indians will be able to live with the rest of us on equal terms, compete on equal terms and become indistinguishable from other Canadian citizens. That, it seems to me, should be our ultimate goal. By that I do not mean to suggest for one minute-I have been warned about this-that anyone has the slightest thought of taking away from the Indians any of their treaty rights, traditional rights, or anything they feel especially belongs to them, or of using any form of compulsion whatsoever to make them change faster than they are willing to change. I think the task is to try to persuade them that by changing, by improving, by becoming educated, they will have a better way of life. This is not going to be easy.
One thing I appreciated very much in what was said by the hon. member for The Battlefords was the tribute he paid to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. It is true. In my very limited experience of visiting

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to extend the discussion of this subject at any length, but I should like to mention one or two points arising out of my observation of the situation in respect of the Indians in the area from which I come. I remember visiting one of the Indian villages during last summer. I made some comment to the chief, who was showing me around, that the children looked to be quite healthy. I still remember clearly the gleam that came into his eye when he pointed out to me that for the first time within his memory, and he was not a young man, the population of his little tribal group was on the increase instead of the reverse being true.
I also had the opportunity of visiting two or three of the schools, and I must say I was very pleased with the type of buildings and the equipment that appeared to be available in schools in fairly isolated locations. Certainly to my way of thinking they compared quite favourably with the general public schools of that district on the coast of British Columbia.
There is one matter of policy on which I should like a word of clarification from the minister, if he is in a position to give it. It has to do with a subject on which he only touched in his recent remarks, the question of when our Indians become full citizens of the country. Perhaps I might put the question in the form of a riddle. When is a fisherman not a fisherman on the coast of British Columbia? I suggest that possibly the answer to that might be, when he is an Indian.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: Or when he does not catch fish.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
The reason I have put the matter in that way is that I should like to know first of all whether there is a policy and, if so, what is the policy with respect to the construction of certain works in connection with fishing operations and that sort of thing in the coastal areas of British Columbia? About a year ago I had occasion to look into a proposal for providing certain facilities which fishermen need for tying up their boats and so on. I must say that a very thorough investigation was made of the project, but I shall not go into any of the details. I discovered that in this particular case if the


project had been proceeded with it would have been constructed by the federal department of works, but that the funds would have come from the money provided for the Indian affairs branch.
On the other hand I know of other instances, and I can mention one example, where that was not the case. There is an item appearing in the details on page 498 of the estimates book, under public works, harbours and rivers engineering branch, which provides for breakwater repairs at a location which is definitely in Indian territory.
I should like to know whether there is any general policy in respect to where the line is drawn, or whether the policy is perhaps made on an ad hoc basis. I should like to know whether this matter has been discussed among the Indian affairs branch, the Department of Public Works and possibly, as I suggested, the Department of Fisheries. Is there any real policy in respect of that, or is it something that has not been clarified? If there is a policy, could the minister tell us briefly what that policy has been or is likely to be?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: That is a question to which I should really like to give consideration before answering. If the hon. gentleman would not mind letting me give the answer at a later time, I shall undertake to do that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: That would be quite satisfactory to me, Mr. Chairman. It is something that I feel would be useful to know in the event of other matters coming to my attention or that of the other members who live in coastal areas in which these problems are apt to arise.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: I am going to be quite brief, Mr. Chairman, so I do not want you to look glumly at me. I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that I have one Indian and one reserve in my constituency. I am speaking now of the sole survivor of the Arrow Lake band and the Arrow Lake Indian reserve. It is a small reserve in a very beautiful spot on the lake. I am just bringing this to the minister's attention, and asking if it is possible for a few other families to be brought in to utilize that beautiful reserve on a lovely bay with a sandy beach. There may be a possibility of bringing some other Kootenay Indians in there so they could enjoy the facilities, and continue the reserve as the Arrow Lake reserve. I just bring that to his attention.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext: I shall have a look at the matter.

Education-
78.	Administration, operation and maintenance, $8,521,245.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE COST OF LOANS
speechtext:
There are a few brief comments I want to make on this item. I have listened carefully to everything that has been said thus far in this discussion. I would agree that this item concerning education is crucial in everything that has taken place here this evening. I appreciated the information that was revealed in our discussions in the estimates committee on this topic of Indian affairs. It was also encouraging to note the minister's emphasis then, and again tonight, on the need to gradually move away from paternalism by gradually breaking down the segregation of our Indian population.
In this connection I would say that education is fundamentally important. It seems to me that the emphasis on establishing day schools on the reserves rather than depending upon residential schools is important in this whole process. During the Easter recess I took the opportunity of visiting two reserves in my own constituency to see the sort of activity that was taking place out there. I am glad to see this move toward establishing schools on the reserves, and I would merely say that I hope the educational program carried on there will be just as broad as possible under the circumstances. I hope it can include the adult population as well as the juvenile population, because an adult education program goes hand in hand with breaking down this segregation.
Finally there is the matter of coeducation which is also proceeding; that is, the mixing of white and Indian children in the same schools. I investigated the situation in my own city of Brandon, and I found that the superintendent of education is very keen about this coeducational program. He is anxious to promote it just as far as is possible. However, he had one small complaint. He finds there are not sufficient students of high school age arriving at the local residential school to incorporate into the city high school program. There was a feeling this might arise as a result of a certain misunderstanding and difference of interpretation between the local superintendent of schools and the superintendent of Indian schools.
In summing up, I would say I do agree that we are moving in the right direction in connection with this problem. If what we have on paper is vigorously implemented in the years that lie ahead, we will gradually work toward the desired goal of uniting the Indians with the general population.

speechtext: I have just a short comment on this item. I do not want to hold up the committee at all, but I should like to say that these cash accounts, as they are called, are quite confusing both to the house and to the general public. For instance, it was intimated in the estimates of 1952-53 that the estimates totalled $406,000. Actually the amount spent was roughly $108,000 out of this purchase account; that was just the amount spent, and this actually was charged up in the estimates. Conversely, in the year 1953-54 there was $490,000 in the estimates and the amount spent was $699. My only point in bringing this to the attention of the house is that I do not think the estimates as they are presently drawn give a true picture of the estimates and expenditures.
